items.descriptionTR:
Renewable energy could help African food businesses boost productivity and competitiveness, but the upfront cost, fragmented markets and limited financing stand in the way
The post More support needed to power Africa’s food systems with renewables, experts say appeared first on Climate Home News.
As efforts to expand energy access across Africa grow, experts and policymakers have called this week for greater coordination and investment to power food production with renewables, arguing the sector has been treated separately from energy policy and therefore faces barriers in going green.
Hailemariam Desalegn, former prime minister of Ethiopia, said energy is critical across the food value chain – from irrigation and processing to cold storage and transport – and should therefore be considered a key pillar of strengthening food systems for the future.
“Energy is not separate from the nutrition challenge. Irrigation needs energy. Cold storage, transport, processing, as well as markets – all need reliable energy,” Desalegn told a panel at the 20th session of the Africa Food Systems Forum in Kigali. He said investments in sustainable energy systems could help reduce post-harvest losses and make nutritious food more accessible and affordable.
Africa loses up to 30% of its food before it reaches markets annually, largely due to poor roads, weak storage and inadequate cold chains, according to a 2025 report by the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA).
	•	￼   May 29, 2026  Justice   Q&A: How can African electricity access power jobs not just lightbulbs? Carol Koech from the Global Energy Alliance says electricity connections in Africa should happen in a way that transforms communities and livelihoods  Read more    
	•	￼   Jun 12, 2026  Sponsored   Climate adaptation helps African nations tackle rising conflict over resources The growing overlap between insecurity and climate vulnerability is forcing governments and development agencies to rethink adaptation efforts  Read more    
	•	
Akinyi Walender, Africa director at development charity Practical Action, said poor energy supply in rural communities – where much of Africa’s food is produced – is also limiting productivity. Across the continent, about 600 million people currently live without access to electricity.
“The lack of energy access goes well beyond the inconvenience of not having lighting at home,” Walender said, adding that renewable energy has the potential to power local economies. “When people can access this sort of energy, it can raise rural incomes, improve food security, improve resilience, empower women and stimulate enterprise while creating jobs,” she added. 
Breaking down silos
Unlocking the potential of energy across food systems requires greater coordination, Walender argued, pointing to institutional fragmentation and isolated pilot projects as major barriers. 
“Organisations working on agriculture and energy often operate according to different modalities and the interdependence between agricultural and energy markets is often overlooked,” Walender said, adding that finance institutions also tend to work in silos.
￼
High level dialogue on climate resilience at the Africa Food Systems Forum in Kigali, September, 2026.(Photo: AFS Forum)
Dana Rysankova, global lead for energy access at the World Bank, told a separate event at the forum that the bank is working to break down those barriers through its newly established Productive Use of Energy (PUE) Centre of Excellence based in Nairobi, which has a mandate to foster collaboration and help develop and design programmes across different sectors.
Can giant batteries unlock Africa’s green industrial future?
In June, the World Bank Group and the African Development Bank Group said that over 50 million people had been connected to electricity across 40 African countries under their Mission 300 initiative, which aims to provide electricity access to 300 million Africans by 2030.
Rysankova said the programme has shown that energy access is just the foundation for linking with other sectors to deliver real economic transformation by boosting productivity and local incomes. 
Mission 300 also aims to electrify schools and healthcare services, as well as bringing power to farmers so that they can use it for irrigation, cold storage and other agricultural activities, she added. 
Bridging the finance and infrastructure gap 
Experts said bigger investments are needed in infrastructure and finance to turn energy access into increased productivity and economic value. 
AGRA’s 2026 foresight report, launched at the forum, puts the annual agrifood financing gap at $180 billion, while estimating that closing Africa’s yearly $67 billion-$108 billion shortfall in infrastructure finance could halve post-harvest losses and increase farmer incomes by up to 40%.
However, the cost of transitioning to clean energy is still a major barrier for farmers and agribusinesses.
￼
Delegates at the Africa Food Systems Forum, September, 2026 (Photo: AFS Forum)
￼
Delegates at the Africa Food Systems Forum, September, 2026 (Photo: AFS Forum)
Atinuke Lebile, CEO of Nigerian food processing company Cato Foods, told Climate Home News she would like to switch to using renewables but has been held back by the upfront cost of setting up the systems the firm needs.
Rwandan farmer Gezel also said she would like to invest in a solar irrigation pump, but “it is so expensive”.
Practical Action’s Walender said the challenge is no longer whether solutions exist, but how financial support can reach the communities and businesses where it could have the greatest impact.
“Customers are dispersed and have low incomes. Markets are fragmented, and there are high upfront costs for much energy equipment,” Walender said, adding that financial institutions also often perceive agriculture as a high-risk sector.
Egypt seeks to unlock renewable potential to power regional clean energy hub
For food processing, the business case for using cleaner energy more efficiently is particularly strong, said Vivian Maduekeh of Partners in Food Solutions, which has worked with more than 2,000 companies across Africa.
Maduekeh said food processing firms account for between 42 and 70% of energy use across food systems, while energy represents 15-22% of their total production costs. African food businesses also use roughly twice as much energy per kilogramme of product as their global competitors, putting them at a competitive disadvantage.
The problems they face in shifting to clean energy are “risk, perception of risk and the cost”, she explained, adding that financial mechanisms are needed to help businesses overcome those issues.
Maduekeh encouraged policymakers to consider measures like tax rebates on imported equipment and spending more on research and development to bring down the cost of productive-use technologies.
Making a range of affordable equipment available – such as smaller irrigation pumps – could also help make the transition more accessible, she said. The evidence in favour “is very clear”, she added. “We just need to package it and communicate it to the priorities of investors.”
items.titleTR: More support needed to power Africa’s food systems with renewables, experts say

slots.packetSpot:
One of the practical barriers to access to low-carbon energy in Africa is emerging as financing. In clean cooking, carbon credits are being used as a tool to reduce the cost of electric and efficient biomass stoves for low-income households. According to the Associated Press, governments have secured $900 million in new financing commitments; Kenya-based BURN also subsidizes stoves through carbon credits. Supporters argue that this approach could accelerate access to clean cooking and reduce deforestation and household air pollution; the long-term outcome is seen as dependent on continued demand for high-integrity carbon credits.

In food production and processing, the transition to renewable energy is being discussed as a separate matter of financing and coordination. At the Africa Food Systems Forum in Kigali, Hailemariam Desalegn stressed that the food chain, from irrigation to cold storage and from transport to markets, depends on reliable energy. Akinyi Walender drew attention to inadequate energy supply in rural areas, disconnects between institutions and problems accessing finance.

According to AGRA's 2025 assessment, up to 30 percent of food in Africa is lost before reaching the market. While AGRA's 2026 outlook report estimates the annual agri-food financing gap at $180 billion, the annual gap in infrastructure financing is stated to be between $67 billion and $108 billion. Under the World Bank and African Development Bank Group's Mission 300 initiative, more than 50 million people in 40 African countries have reportedly been connected to electricity; the goal is to provide access to 300 million people by 2030. Nevertheless, system installation costs for farmers and businesses, the affordability of equipment, and financial institutions' view of agriculture as high-risk continue to stand in the way of the transition.
slots.packetTitle: Financing, the bottleneck on the road to clean energy

In Germany, Deutsche Bahn’s corridor renewal plan is being revised around a smaller number of annual works. Palla, who heads the company, said four major renewals a year were too many; in future, they envisage two, or three where technically necessary. slots.packetSpot:
In France, the Church and authorities are expecting record crowds for Pope Leo XIV’s visit from 25 to 28 September. The visit is planned to include stops in Paris, UNESCO headquarters, Lourdes and Metz; Cardinal Jean-Marc Aveline, Archbishop of Marseille and President of the French Bishops’ Conference, is said to have worked to secure the visit.

In Bucharest, meanwhile, thousands are queuing at the New Saint George Church to see a foot fragment said to belong to Saint Anne, brought to Romania for the first time from the Koutloumousiou Monastery on Mount Athos. The Romanian Orthodox Church identifies Saint Anne as the mother of the Virgin Mary; Patriarch Daniel described the opportunity to visit as “a great blessing.” The relics are expected to remain at the church until 10 September, with visiting hours also to be extended for as long as pilgrims continue to arrive.

Data on the prevalence of religious pilgrimages in Romania also point to this interest: according to one study, more than 26 percent of Romanians have gone on pilgrimage at least once. Last year, around 250,000 people visited the relics of Saint Parascheva in Iași; more than 300,000 people attended related religious events. In another survey, 85 percent of respondents described themselves as religious, while 31 percent said they attended church at least once a week.

items.descriptionTR:
A UAE emergency response team has helped to rescue six missing people in Nepal more than two weeks after deadly flash floods struck.
The Emirati search and rescue team, which arrived in the Himalayan country on September 4, joined forces with Nepali authorities to carry out the mission in the Trishuli area.
The humanitarian task force is continuing to support critical operations in Trishuli and Rasuwa, north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu, using advanced equipment and technology.
The team is using drones for surveying, aerial imaging and three-dimensional mapping to aid search and rescue operations and help access targeted locations.
The death toll from the severe floods and mudslides, which swept Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet on August 26, has crossed 1,300, with thousands more still missing.
￼￼￼￼￼￼￼￼
Hammoud Al Afari, director of UAE Relief Operations, said the Emirati team was providing vital knowledge and expertise to Nepali authorities.
The team comprises members of the UAE Joint Operations Command, Dubai Police search and rescue and the UAE Aid Agency. It includes experts in disaster relief, medical evacuation and first aid.
The rescue of the six missing people has brought hope as emergency teams continue to work around the clock and navigate challenging conditions in Nepal.
On Friday, two men were pulled out alive from a tunnel ⁠linked to a hydropower station, nine days after the devastating floods.
Video footage showed the moment Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan were rescued from the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station where they worked, before being airlifted to an army hospital in Kathmandu. The body of a third person was also found.
UAE aid drive
The UAE is continuing to provide essential aid to those worst affected by the floods. Dubai's humanitarian relief hub sent 74 tonnes of aid on Tuesday.
The essential supplies from Dubai Humanitarian – including tents and shelter material, medicine, hygiene kits and winter kits – were airlifted on a Boeing 777-F operated by Emirates SkyCargo to Kathmandu.
The Emirates had already delivered 184 tonnes of aid to Nepal under a $10 million relief response package ordered by President Sheikh Mohamed.
items.titleTR: UAE team helps to rescue six missing 15 days after Nepal's deadly floods

items.descriptionTR:
Dubai's humanitarian relief hub has sent 74 tonnes of critical aid to crisis-hit Nepal to support embattled communities still reeling from the aftermath of deadly floods which struck the country last month.
The essential supplies from Dubai Humanitarian - including tents and shelter materials, medicines, hygiene kits and winter kits - were airlifted on Tuesday aboard a Boeing 777-F operated by Emirates SkyCargo, bound for Kathmandu.
The UAE's latest support for Nepal was sent on the directives of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai.
The cargo comes from the prepositioned stocks of Unicef, the World Food Programme’s United Nations Humanitarian Response Depot (WFP-UNHRD), and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).
“As flood-affected communities in Nepal continue their recovery, this shipment adds to the collective response of the international humanitarian community operating out of Dubai, reaffirming the emirate’s position as a critical link in the global supply chain," said Mohammed Al Shaibani, Chairman of Dubai Humanitarian, said:
"Dubai Humanitarian is also proud of the longstanding partnership with Emirates SkyCargo who have supported and operated this flight given the exceptional emergency circumstances and as part of the country’s response and humanitarian initiatives.
"The dispatch reflects also Dubai Humanitarian’s role as a global hub for pre-positioning, last-mile delivery, and interagency coordination, enabling the quick movement of urgent relief items to communities in need.”
Badr Abbas, divisional senior vice president for Emirates SkyCargo, said the company was committed to supporting those affected by crises across the globe.
“Emirates SkyCargo has a longstanding relationship with Dubai Humanitarian, working side by side to support communities affected by natural disasters and humanitarian crises around the world.
"Our partnership combines Dubai Humanitarian’s expertise in humanitarian relief with Emirates SkyCargo’s network and logistics capabilities to ensure critical aid reaches those who need it the most.
"We are proud to once again support Dubai Humanitarian in this mission, operating a special charter flight to Kathmandu, ensuring life-saving aid can move quickly and efficiently.”
The Emirates has already delivered 184 tonnes of aid to Nepal under a $10 million relief response package ordered by President Sheikh Mohamed.
A glacier collapse and landslide caused flash flooding on August 26, leading to widespread destruction on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
The death toll from the natural disaster has climbed above 1,300, with thousands of people still missing.
An Emirati search and rescue team – which landed in Nepal on Friday – has already begun critical work on the ground in a race against time to save lives.
items.titleTR: Dubai sends 74 tonnes of aid supplies to boost Nepal flood relief effort

items.descriptionTR:
The affluent city-state has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance
Singapore’s prime minister has been given a $1m pay rise as the affluent city-state announced a dramatic one-off salary boost for government ministers.
The pay increases add more than 60% to what are already the world’s highest ministerial salaries.
items.titleTR: Singapore boosts PM’s salary by $1m amid major pay rise for ministers

slots.packetSpot:
Under the new framework approved by the Singapore government, the pay of political office-holders will rise by up to 9%. With the change expected to take effect on 15 October following recommendations by an independent review committee, the annual salary of a minister at the lowest MR4 grade will reach about S$1.2 million, or US$0.95 million. This will be the first change to ministerial salaries since 2011.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said during the parliamentary debate that no one should enter politics for money. According to Wong, who argued that the PAP government does not use high pay to attract candidates, competitive salaries can allow people who already want to serve the public to enter politics without completely upending their legitimate financial responsibilities to their families.

Wong said he would donate the entirety of the increase in his own salary, including the associated tax benefits, for five years. He also said the new pay benchmarks would not be adopted immediately; salaries would rise gradually depending on individual performance and responsibilities. He added that he could consider disclosing more information on the distribution of salaries and performance bonuses.
slots.packetTitle: Pay rises, but not politics for profit

The overnight visitor levy means places will get rewarded for doing what they need to attract more visitors and grow their local economies.
Labour’s solution to every issue is always to hike taxes. This is just the latest method they’ve found to squeeze more money out of hardworking families and the economy.
The hospitality industry has already been hit by colossal business rates hikes thanks to Labour, on top of their Jobs Tax and employment red tape that have driven up costs. Now hotels and other businesses face another blow that will harm local economies and discourage local tourism. VAT is already charged at 20% on hotels - much higher than in other countries - and now they’ll pay VAT on this tourism tax too: a Labour double whammy.
items.titleTR: No 10 defends plan for visitor tax, saying communities will keep ‘more of the benefits of tourism’ – UK politics live

slots.packetSpot:
Mayors in England are set to be given the power to impose a visitor levy on paid overnight stays. According to Downing Street, the optional tax will be calculated as a percentage of the accommodation cost rather than as a flat amount; while no upper limit for the rate has been announced, it is expected to be kept proportionate.

Shelters and refuges will automatically be exempt; mayors will be able to set other exemptions, including for campsites. Plans for how the revenues will be used are expected to be submitted by March 2028. The government sees the measure as a first step in devolving fiscal powers and says more of the benefit generated by tourism will remain in local communities.

While some mayors, local government bodies and a charity working to protect the Lake District support the proposal, the Confederation of British Industry and ABTA are concerned about its possible effects on the tourism sector, competitiveness and the administrative burden on businesses. It is not yet clear whether areas without a mayor will be able to use this power, or whether the tax can be applied only in certain parts of a region.
slots.packetTitle: Should tourism's proceeds stay local?

items.descriptionTR: [Nile Post] Government has dismissed reports circulating on social media that Tooro Queen Mother Best Kemigisha has been placed under house arrest amid growing tensions and divisions within the kingdom following the death of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.
items.titleTR: Uganda: Government Dismisses Claims Tooro Queen Mother Is Under House Arrest

items.descriptionTR: KAMPALA, Sept 10 - The traditional Ugandan kingdom of Tooro was plunged into a bitter succession battle on Thursday after the family of the late king, Oyo Nyimba, rejected clan members' choice of a television news anchor to succeed him.
items.titleTR: Ugandan kingdom gripped by succession battle after monarch's death

slots.packetSpot:
A succession dispute has come to the fore in the Kingdom of Tooro following reports that King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV died in the United States. The royal clan’s succession committee announced that it had selected Oyo’s cousin, Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as the new king. By contrast, Princess Ruth Komuntale and Queen Anne Best Kemigisha said a 2022 will identifies Oyo’s legally recognised biological son as heir to the throne; the child’s identity has not been disclosed publicly.

Security measures around the palace are another point of dispute. Kemigisha alleged that the family is being held under house arrest, that soldiers have surrounded the palace and that royal guards were removed without prior notice. The Ugandan government rejected the claim as baseless, while explaining the deployment as a precaution against possible unrest and calling for restraint. Oyo’s funeral is scheduled to take place on Saturday at the Karambi Royal Tombs.
slots.packetTitle: A throne in mourning in Tooro

Turning Point USA, the slain conservative activist’s organization, is widely expected to back the current vice president
An empty chair at the American Airlines Center recalled Charlie Kirk on Wednesday during the first Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas. “Charlie! Charlie!” thousands of attendees chanted as President Donald Trump hailed the slain conservative activist as a martyr and urged his followers to honor his legacy at the polls in November. items.titleTR: A year after Charlie Kirk's death, Turning Point USA grows but Trump slips with young voters

items.descriptionTR: The assassination sent shockwaves through the conservative youth movement, which students say has lost momentum and a vital figurehead.
items.titleTR: Year after Charlie Kirk's death, conservative students struggle to fill void he left

slots.packetSpot:
A year after Charlie Kirk was fatally shot at Utah Valley University, Turning Point USA says it has expanded its high school and college chapters. According to the organization’s figures, it has more than 3,500 high school clubs and more than 1,500 college chapters; dozens of new chapters are reported to have opened in West Virginia, while teams in Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa are also said to have been strengthened. Erika Kirk serves as chief executive.

By contrast, it remains unclear who or what will replace Kirk’s personal influence. Fluctuating attendance at campus events, internal friction, the departure of some chapters and unfounded conspiracy claims concerning Kirk’s killing are among the points of tension among young conservatives. J. D. Vance stands out as a possible Republican candidate whom Kirk and Turning Point USA planned to support for 2028; however, there is no official candidacy.

Donald Trump commemorated Kirk at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas and said he had helped draw young men to the party. Polls, meanwhile, show that issues such as the cost of living, the war with Iran and relations with Israel are eroding support for Trump among some young voters. As organizational expansion continues, the political allegiance of this young base and the movement’s shared direction have yet to become clear.
slots.packetTitle: The void inside the growing structure

items.descriptionTR:
Is Donald Trump trying to help Republicans win the midterm elections? The obvious answer to this question is yes, of course, simply because all political leaders benefit from their party winning elections. Yet several of Trump’s actions throw this normally perfunctory question into at least some doubt.
Traditionally, candidates laboring under the burden of an unpopular president seek to detach themselves from the national brand. Trump is making this impossible. He has launched a national ad campaign focused on himself, and thrown a high-profile “midterm convention” designed to further reinforce the synonymity of the party and its leader. Trump has also made several remarks that convey an emotional detachment from the election’s outcome—comments such as “I’m not affected by the election” or “I don’t care about the midterms.”
Perhaps he is merely feigning indifference. Maybe he truly does not care. More likely, Trump cares about the outcome, but not enough to permit Republicans to acknowledge his lack of popularity. His approach, at any rate, nicely illustrates the drawbacks of handing total control of a political party to an egomaniac.
Midterm elections have historically disfavored the president’s party. Candidates for office who are running in neutral or hostile territory accordingly tend to emphasize their differences with the president—think of Joe Manchin running an ad in West Virginia in 2010 showing him firing an actual bullet at Barack Obama’s cap-and-trade bill, or the Republican Will Hurd in 2018 criticizing Trump’s racism and affinity for Russia.
[Listen: Trump’s economy goes to the polls]
Trump’s public standing is unusually dire. He is currently polling far worse than either he did at this point in 2018 or Joe Biden did four years ago. In theory, this ought to give Republicans an especially strong incentive to edge away from Trump and emphasize local themes in their elections.
Trump has decided to block this escape route. He is commandeering earned media with his “Trumpapalooza” show, drawing attention to the person endangered Republicans desperately need their constituents to forget. He has hoarded the party’s ad budget, warning Republicans, “This is my money that I control,” and that he would spend it on “Republicans that I think are good,” which is to say, slavishly loyal. He has promised to barnstorm the country, telling reporters, “I’ll be making a lot of stops,” including in Alaska, where the Republican Dan Sullivan is trailing.
There is an old Simpsons episode in which the elderly oligarch Montgomery Burns informs the obsequious Smithers that, upon his own death, his loyal aide will be buried alive at his boss’s feet. Trump appears to be thinking along similar lines.
This self-defeating behavior makes a degree of sense if you accept that Trump’s interest in politics is purely egocentric. He has difficulty caring about anything that does not directly involve himself, and the prospect of Republicans holding seats by repudiating his record is likely unpalatable.
The benefits of same-party control of Congress are also smaller for Trump than other presidents, because he governs mainly through executive action. To the extent that a Democratic majority in either chamber might threaten him with oversight, he will surely disregard it, as he did during his first term. Although he finds Republican majorities preferable, the size of those majorities matters to him far less than their composition—a fully loyal minority may seem preferable to a fractious majority.
What makes less sense is the willingness of many Republicans to cooperate with a strategy that consigns many of them to defeat.
Consider, for instance, Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan. Rogers came up through politics long before Trump entered it, and is trying to win office in a state where the president’s approval rating is 25 points underwater. A recent poll of the state found Trump’s endorsement made voters less likely, by a 55 percent to 27 percent margin, to support a candidate. Yet Rogers has opened no daylight whatsoever with the unpopular president, even echoing his false claims of having the 2020 election stolen from him. When Trump launched a trade war with Canada, a move that poses an especially dire threat to Rogers’s own state, he declined to take the opportunity to display independence. Instead, he issued a statement mumbling his approval. (“President Trump is right to put America First—and tariffs are necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution.”) The same dynamic is occurring in other races, where Trump is throwing himself behind incumbents who are in danger mainly because voters don’t like him.
[Read: Trump plans to buy midterm ads about his own record]
To be sure, some Republicans subscribe to the theory that the Trump era has suspended normal midterm election dynamics. According to this account, a decisive sliver of voters are loyal to Trump, and not his party. Republicans can win only by enticing them to vote, which means making the election about their hero. “We’ve seen that a lot of Trump voters—they will crawl over glass to vote for the president,” one Republican strategist explained to Politico.
Yet Trump has tried before to insert himself into non-presidential elections. And his efforts have mostly failed—not only in the 2018 midterms, when he refused to lie low, but also in multiple off-schedule elections (the most famous case being Georgia’s 2021 Senate runoff, which he made into a referendum on his effort to overturn the 2020 election). In the Trump era, his party has fared well only when it has been able to focus on the shortcomings of unpopular Democratic opponents, such as Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Biden and Kamala Harris in 2024. Making elections about Trump—which also occurred when he ran for reelection in 2020—has been a losing gambit.
The political tip sheets in recent days have been filled with the lamentations of fatalistic Republican operatives. “We have no choice. We’re stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not,” a top Republican campaign official confessed to Axios. They cannot stop Trump from staging Trumpapalooza, so they are reduced to praying for low ratings. “My only hope is that no one watches it since it’s competing versus NFL opening games,” a person close to the White House told Politico. “Hopefully nobody notices the embarrassing show.” Republicans are cooperating in a strategy that sacrifices their best chance of political survival, because the past decade has trained them to believe that resistance to Trump is futile.
Trump did far less damage to the country during his first term, both because institutions and norm-following officials restrained him, and because his pathological instincts frequently undermined his support. The former limitation has broken down in the second term, but the latter one remains. Trump’s support has collapsed in large part because of his own poor choices.
Traditionally, candidates try to distance themselves from unpopular presidents. But this year, that’s impossible.
items.titleTR: Does Trump Want Republicans to Win the Midterms?

items.descriptionTR: Republicans hope to build momentum as they sag in the polls ahead of November's midterm election, but some vulnerable candidates skip the event.
items.titleTR: Fewer than half of vulnerable congressional candidates have speaking roles at GOP convention

slots.packetSpot:
As the 2026 US midterm elections approach, Donald Trump is taking centre stage in the party's election campaign through a national advertising campaign, the Republican convention in Dallas and planned campaign stops. This visibility is bringing to the fore the question of how far Republican candidates, particularly in competitive races, can distance themselves from Trump.

At the two-day convention in Dallas, 19 candidates were scheduled to speak, according to CNBC's review of the 45 most competitive House and Senate races. While Mike Rogers was on the programme, numerous vulnerable Republican candidates chose to skip the event, according to MS NOW. The convention's overlap with the opening games of the NFL's 2026 season was also cited among the logistical and scheduling challenges facing the organisation.

Trump's control over the advertising budget, his remarks linking his support for candidates to loyalty, and his promise to make stops across the country, including in Alaska, are increasing the campaign's personal weight. Its effect on election results, and whether this approach will help or harm candidates, have not been determined.
slots.packetTitle: The midterm stage in Trump's shadow

items.descriptionTR: Half of Europeans cannot picture a credible path to a stronger EU, an “imagination gap” that risks ceding the political initiative to nostalgic far‑right forces, according to a major new study by the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR).
items.titleTR: Europe’s ‘imagination gap’ risks empowering far right, survey warns

items.descriptionTR:
Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generation
Not all that long ago, Europe was a beacon of liberal idealism. One memoir recalls it as an era “comfortably saturated with confidence in the unfailing and binding power of tolerance and conciliation”. The economic system seemed obviously preferable to barbarous alternatives. “People honestly believed that the divergencies and the boundaries between nations and sects would gradually melt away into a common humanity,” the author added.
Those words could describe the spirit of globalisation at the turn of the millennium. They were written in the 1930s by Stefan Zweig, reflecting on the optimism of late 19th-century Vienna from the perspective of a Jewish émigré whose world had been destroyed by murderous nationalism. Zweig took his own life in 1942. He never saw fascism defeated. He couldn’t have imagined a renaissance of liberalism in the second half of the 20th century so complete as to attain a pitch of complacency rivalling the one he remembered from his childhood.
items.titleTR: European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss | Rafael Behr

slots.packetSpot:
Research by the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), based on 5,834 AI-moderated interviews conducted in Britain, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Poland, finds that 68 percent of participants define Europe through decline or a “lost normality”; 12 percent speak of awakening or renewal. According to the research, nearly three-quarters of participants think Europe is handling its main problems poorly.

The study states that those who want more Europe but doubt that leaders can deliver it make up a segment of roughly one-third. Slow decision-making, the perception of double standards, the belief that Europe yields to stronger powers, anxiety about war, dependence on the US and the rise of the far right are counted among the main sources of these doubts. It warns that an inability to imagine a credible future could increase receptiveness to far-right narratives that present the past as the future.

Rafael Behr, meanwhile, argues that liberal idealism is under pressure from far-right parties, MAGA ideology and allegations concerning Kremlin money. The reported success of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France and Nigel Farage’s politics in Britain stand out as different manifestations of nationalist forces’ efforts to exploit the political space opening up in Europe.
slots.packetTitle: In search of a credible future

items.descriptionTR:
Arun Arora, bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, condemns ‘twisted theology’ of groups who demonstrated at south coast ports at weekend
	•	UK politics live – latest updates
Fascism is on the rise in the UK, a Church of England bishop has warned, condemning the “twisted theology” of the self-described “Christian patriots” who demonstrated at ports on the south coast last weekend.
The masked, black-clad, anti-migrant agitators – led by Daniel “Danny Tommo” Thomas, a former bodyguard of the far-right influencer Tommy Robinson – were heard chanting: “Christ is King.”
items.titleTR: Fascism on the rise in the UK, Anglican bishop says

items.descriptionTR:
Last weekend was gloriously sunny in the south of England, and my family attended a friend’s birthday party on the outskirts of Dover.
The historic port stands beneath magnificent white chalk cliffs and has always been busy since it’s home to the shortest British sea crossing to France. There are, therefore, often long lines of lorries coming into Dover port from all over Europe, car ferries for holidaymakers and enormous cruise ships.
As I drove to the birthday party, it seemed England was at its best. Warm sunshine lit up the French coast about 40 kilometres away across a calm blue sea. Then radio news reports spoke of something much less appealing, a bizarre demonstration of about 250 men in black masks, black anoraks, black jeans and boots marching up and down, blocking the road to the port entrance.
A friend from Dover who witnessed the demonstration told me they were a far-right group from across south-eastern England. He described them as “neo-Nazis” who followed shouted commands from their leader. This port-blocking parade was potentially threatening. It mobilised Kent police and made national news headlines. The demonstrators described themselves as English “patriots” with “a fierce love for our homeland”, though why “love” involved stopping lorries and holidaymakers was not explained.
￼
A video posted on social media by the group’s presumed “leader” dripped with vague menace: “Very, very soon, we are going to send a message that will make sure they understand that we will not go down without a fight. We will not allow our nation to be plagued in the way that it is.” It’s not clear who “they” are or who would “understand” what, or what the “plague” involved, but it sounded like classic far-right anti-immigrant whingeing mixed with threats of unspecified bad things to come.
The idea of weird masked men in black clothes shambling around a sea harbour to “defend” England would be laughable if it were not also so threatening. In recent years, far-right anti-migrant demonstrations across the UK ranged from Belfast to Southport and elsewhere. Some involved riots and arson, but many of these pretend English “patriots” also turned out to be men with criminal convictions including for domestic violence against women.
No arrests were made at Dover, and the masked mob marched to the train station and left. But this was a reminder that the traditional rather sober British political right and some new far right disruptors are a discordant, divided bunch.
￼
The traditional Conservative party of the centre-right, led by Kemi Badenoch, suffered a big dip in the polls but is now recovering. To Ms Badenoch’s right, Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party is, however, showing signs of distress. Reform, once leading in opinion polls, is enduring damaging publicity, media investigations and political blunders. A sting by undercover reporters showed two key Reform figures, close to Mr Farage, seriously embarrassing the party over potential donations that may be considered illegal.
We shall see. Mr Farage was at least forced publicly to admit that comments by the two key aides – James Orr and Dan Jukes – filmed by the undercover team were “injudicious at best”. The party has now suspended both men. Mr Farage himself is under continuing investigation over his acceptance of a £5 million (about $6.7 million) gift from a resident of Thailand and other matters.
Moreover, Reform’s chief selling point was that it is different from the old Conservative party and “politics as usual”. Well, yes, but possibly not in a good way. Reform has slipped in opinion polls. And it’s difficult to pretend to be “new” and “different” when Reform’s key figures include former MPs who defected from the traditional Conservative party. These include Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman, both former Conservative cabinet ministers who switched when Reform was rising in opinion polls.
￼
Now Reform is slipping, and the Conservatives may recover, but either way the right-of-centre vote is split.
The Dover demonstrators appear way beyond the normal right-wing spectrum. In their black garb they looked like a particularly scruffy re-incarnation of the English fascist party of the 1930s, Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts. Maybe the Dover demonstrators should be called the “Black Anoraks” or “Black Trainers” given their choice of clothing. Besides, wearing a mask on a sunny day suggests you may have something to hide. My Dover resident friend who witnessed the demonstration said he felt a real sense of threat to peace in his community.
What we can say for sure is that after a significant loss of voter support, the longstanding centre-right Conservative party appears to have stabilised. Ms Badenoch has made changes to her team and the party’s poll ratings are improving. Mr Farage’s “breaking the mould” of British politics has turned into a different question – “did he break electoral law?” And the 250 far-right masked “Black Anoraks” in Dover may seem not only a modern echo of the 1930s fascist Blackshirts but a potential threat to public order, raising serious questions about the toxic edge of British politics.
items.titleTR: Britain’s political right is splitting – even as its toxic fringe is growing

slots.packetSpot:
Actions by masked, black-clad anti-immigrant groups in Dover and Portsmouth brought concerns over the visibility of the far right in the United Kingdom to the fore. A demonstration of around 250 people that blocked the road leading to the port entrance in Dover prompted Kent Police to respond; no arrests were made, and the group later went to the train station and dispersed.

The Bishop of Kirkstall, Arun Arora, condemned the actions, also taking aim at the language used by “Christian patriots”, and described them as part of a worrying increase in attempts to tear apart the social fabric. Arora warned that nationalism, racism and intimidation pose a threat to social cohesion; the Archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, also said that Christian leaders have a responsibility to speak out against intimidation.

The appearance of the group in Dover is being compared with Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts of the 1930s. At the same time, competition between the centre-right Conservative Party and Reform UK continues: James Orr and Dan Jukes were suspended by Reform UK following a report made using covert filming; Nigel Farage, meanwhile, is under investigation over a £5 million donation reportedly received from a person living in Thailand and other matters.
slots.packetTitle: In the shadow of black clothing

Bucharest authorities expand investigation into the controversial 'manosphere' influencers, bringing new human trafficking charges against Andrew and Tristan Tate.
items.titleTR: Romania Opens New Human Trafficking Case Against Tate Brothers

items.descriptionTR: A federal judge denied them bail, saying the dual US-UK citizens' wealth and frequent international travel "constitute quintessential flight risks".
items.titleTR: Tate brothers to remain in US jail as they fight extradition to UK

slots.packetSpot:
Andrew and Tristan Tate are simultaneously at the centre of a new child-trafficking indictment in Romania and extradition proceedings to the United Kingdom in the United States. Romanian organised-crime prosecutors charged the two brothers, along with two Romanian nationals, in a new case involving related allegations including child trafficking and money laundering. The brothers have been under investigation in Romania since their detention in December 2022; they deny the charges.

The new case, opened after the Bucharest Court of Appeal returned the previous case to prosecutors for the investigation to be conducted again, forms a separate track in the Romanian proceedings. While the brothers are in the United States, a federal judge in Miami denied their bail requests as they continue to challenge possible extradition to the United Kingdom. The judge cited their wealth, frequent international travel, foreign connections and limited ties to the United States as grounds for a risk of flight.

United Kingdom authorities announced a total of 59 charges, including rape, offences linked to sex trafficking and charges involving indecent images of a child; they have until 16 September to submit a full extradition request. Romanian authorities also alleged that there had been attempts to influence victims' statements during the previous investigation; at the same time, they stated that the brothers had complied with the obligations imposed on them throughout the process. The Tate brothers' lawyers say they will mount a defence in the legal proceedings in each jurisdiction; the brothers deny all charges and allegations.
slots.packetTitle: The Tate brothers in a three-country legal squeeze

items.descriptionTR:
Spiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence
	•	‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctions
Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.
The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described UK sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.
items.titleTR: Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements

items.descriptionTR: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has defended the decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank
items.titleTR: UK government defends decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements

slots.packetSpot:
Britain has decided to ban imports of all goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to block financing, construction, infrastructure, real estate and advertising services linked to the settlements. Ed Miliband defended the measure, which is expected to take effect within no more than nine months; he said the arms embargo had also been tightened to cover weapons “materially connected” to Gaza and the occupation.

Miliband used the term “ethnic cleansing” in relation to settler violence and the displacement of Palestinians. Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis described the decision as “gesture politics” that could strengthen the extremism it targets. Miliband said he respected Mirvis but disagreed with that assessment.

Prominent Israeli figures including David Harel, Ehud Olmert, Dan Halutz, Yuli Tamir, Roni Bar-On, Yoram Ben Zeev, Nadav Tamir and Avraham Burg reportedly supported or welcomed the targeted measures. Fourteen Israeli human rights organisations also welcomed the decision. This support differs from a comprehensive boycott of Israel: Harel said he opposed sanctions targeting the state as a whole, while supporting measures directed at practices in the West Bank.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar condemned the decision. Israel reportedly closed Britain’s consulate in East Jerusalem, prevented British MPs and other British citizens from entering the country, and announced or threatened certain restrictions on bilateral cooperation. While France and Canada announced that they were planning similar steps, other European countries were said to have taken or been considering similar measures.

Exports from the settlements to Britain were reportedly $45 million last year, within the total $4.4 billion volume of goods and services trade between Britain and Israel. The direct economic impact is therefore expected to remain limited; however, sanctions against companies that finance or facilitate settlement expansion are said to be capable of having broader consequences.
slots.packetTitle: The line drawn around settlement trade

items.descriptionTR:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
When Donald Trump looks at a map, he doesn’t see nations. He sees property. All of those pretty colors do not represent actual places filled with human beings who have distinct cultures, languages, and histories; the planet, to Trump, is a big board game, like Risk or Monopoly. Greenland isn’t a real location—it’s a valuable chunk of territory nestled between Boardwalk and Park Place. The Strait of Hormuz isn’t an international waterway—it’s a thing to control somewhere between Kamchatka and East Africa.
This inability to grasp the existence of independent nations drives the president to fury when countries and their governments refuse to play along with his delusions. Trump cannot understand why Iran won’t bend to his will, why NATO won’t instantly obey his orders, why South Korea and Japan won’t just write checks or provide troops on demand. The only people Trump seems to respect are the autocrats in Beijing and Moscow and Pyongyang who, like him, view the world as a brutal competition for power and territory.
Now Trump has declared economic war on Canada, a nation that has vexed him for years. Even by the standards of Trump’s many fixations, his obsession with Canada has become not only weird but truly destructive. He has opened a giant political and economic rift with one of America’s biggest trading partners, a sister nation, and an ally in the common defense of North America and Europe. Why does Trump hate Canada so much?
We can only speculate about what goes on in the president’s head, but his actions suggest a pattern. When Trump is frustrated about something he can’t control, he lashes out at friends harder than he does enemies. He took out his anger about the Epstein files on legislators from his own party, even though he had campaigned on releasing those documents. Stymied by Iran on multiple fronts, Trump decided to blame South Korea for not helping him, and curtailed military exercises with a vital U.S. ally. (This decision also had the side benefit of allowing Trump to make another embarrassing overture to the North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, a bromantic gesture that went unreciprocated.) Trump values absolute loyalty over everything else—not that he always returns it—and he detests any sign that others, especially those who are supposed to be his friends and allies, might have views and interests of their own.
The American economy is stalling, and Trump’s poll numbers are in the basement, so the next obvious move is to pick a huge fight with a nation that is essentially family to Americans. Canada is most definitely a foreign country, which is one reason I like to visit. (Go ahead—try to find a convenience store in America that sells Aero chocolate bars or wine gums.) But to the utterly incurious Trump, it probably looks like an extension of upstate New York.
Canada and America are bound by deep cultural and historical bonds, but ironically, the superficial similarities are likely driving much of Trump’s vitriol. How dare these people—whose country is, to him, just a cheap knockoff of America—defy him! After all, most of Canada speaks English; its cities look like ours (if definitely cleaner); we share pop stars and TV shows; they even call their money “the dollar,” despite its colorful look and plasticky feel. Canada, in the president’s eyes, is less a sovereign nation than a real-estate parcel he forgot to buy because it’s in a neighborhood he never visits.
The fact that Canada is led by someone Trump accidentally helped put in office probably irks him too. Early last year, Canada’s Liberal Party had been in power for 10 years and was facing a huge defeat in what seemed to be an impending “change” election. Trump, as usual, could not control himself when it came to the internal politics of an allied nation: He imposed tariffs during the lead-up to the Canadian vote while banging on about making Canada the 51st state. The Liberal leader Mark Carney—an unflappable public figure who is completely different from Trump in both temperament and intellect—pivoted quickly and campaigned on standing up to the American president. Carney almost overnight went from a no-hoper to prime minister. And now he has shown that he is perfectly willing to retaliate against Trump’s policies rather than fold. If Trump wants tariffs, Carney will provide them—in spades.
Imagine how all of this looks to Trump, who has made clear that Canada shouldn’t even exist as an independent state. I am humiliated as an American, and as a friend of Canada, to admit this, but Trump’s attitude toward Canada is almost indistinguishable from the way Russian President Vladimir Putin sees Ukraine: not as a state but as some kind of historical anomaly that should be returned to its rightful owners. Trump might think it’s funny to post memes of Canada with an American flag superimposed on it, but those jokes are a lot less hilarious to people in places such as Ukraine, who are fighting a war against a dictator who feels exactly the same way about their country.
Canadians are probably scratching their head over Trump’s willingness to hurt his own people and especially his own party. Trump may hate Canada, but it’s hard to imagine what he thinks he’ll gain by causing economic pain to Americans along the Canadian border, especially in states such as Maine and Michigan, where Republicans are facing tight battles for congressional seats. What the Canadians may not realize is that, with this president, none of it has to make sense, and that if recent history is a guide, he will back down, perhaps after declaring victory over Ottawa. Trump will then move on, leaving ordinary Americans and their Canadian friends to deal with the damage.

The Anniversary I Wish I Didn’t Share With My Husband
By Ellen S. Bakalian
During a visit in May to the Maritime Museum in Halifax, Nova Scotia, I watched a film about a 1917 cargo-ship explosion that killed more than 1,700 townspeople and injured many more. The grainy black-and-white images of the flattened city catapulted me back to the devastation of Lower Manhattan after terrorists attacked the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. Halifax suffered a blizzard following the cargo-ship catastrophe, and the sight of the city covered in a deep blanket of snow recalled the dust and debris from the once-glimmering towers that coated the Financial District. When I heard the recorded voices of the Haligonian survivors recounting their memories, I walked out of the small theater to cry.
Twenty-five years on from September 11, 2001, an image or memory can still evoke the very moment I learned that my 36-year-old redheaded husband, Jeffrey R. Smith, would not be coming home from work that day.

items.titleTR: Is Canada Strengthening Its ‘Middle Power’ Strategy Against the US?

slots.packetSpot:
Economic and political tensions between the United States and Canada are bringing Ottawa's search to reduce its dependence on Washington to the fore. Donald Trump's tariffs and rhetoric toward Canada have increased uncertainty in the long-standing economic and political partnership between the two countries; the Mark Carney administration, alongside retaliatory measures, is moving to broaden its trade and diplomatic options.

The United States remains Canada's most important economic and security partner. Ottawa's aim, however, is not to sever ties or form an anti-US bloc; it is to reduce the vulnerability created by excessive dependence on a single market and great power. Engagement with China, India, Europe and Africa is taking shape as part of this search for diversification.

According to Canada's High Commissioner to South Africa, James Christoff, roughly two-thirds of the country's economy depends on international trade. Ottawa aims to double its exports outside the United States over the next decade and for this to generate approximately $300 billion in additional trade; exports outside the United States are also reported to have increased by $33 billion over the past year. The idea of establishing separate cooperation with different countries in trade, energy, security, climate and technology is emerging as a flexible middle-power strategy aimed at expanding Canada's room for manoeuvre.
slots.packetTitle: Ottawa puts distance between itself and Washington

items.descriptionTR:
Leaders of the Brics group are to gather in New Delhi this weekend at a time of uncertainty in the global economy, with the Iran war disrupting energy markets, trade routes and long-standing relationships.
Six months of war in the Middle East has forced countries to rethink where they get their energy, how they move goods and how they do business.
The summit, on September 12 and 13, comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration steps up an economic campaign to isolate Iran, warning its trading partners that they could face secondary sanctions if they maintain financial ties with Tehran. At the same time, the conflict has disrupted the flow of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices higher.
The strait, a strategic waterway through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the war in February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US blockade of Iranian ports.
The new US front is called Operation Economic Outcast. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US planned initially to target banks and has urged other countries to sever economic ties with Iran or risk losing access to the dollar-based financial system. That puts some Brics members in a difficult position.
China is Iran’s biggest oil customer, taking more than 80 per cent of its shipped crude. Washington's campaign has already disrupted Iranian oil exports, while Chinese buyers – Iran's main remaining customers – face increasing scrutiny.
Iranian crude loadings fell in August to about 260,000 barrels per day, from about 1.7 million bpd a year earlier, according to data from commodity analytics firm Kpler. Only a trickle is still moving off terminals for distribution by lorry, train or smaller boats over the Caspian ⁠Sea.
The US policy also puts countries such as India in an awkward situation. New Delhi remains a critical US partner in the Indo-Pacific, but it also has commercial and strategic interests in Iran that it is unlikely to readily abandon.
A week after the Trump administration launched its new sanctions campaign, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan. It was their first meeting since the war broke out.
The UAE, once one of Iran’s most important commercial gateways, suspended financial and economic transactions with Tehran last month following regional escalation. Iran retaliated against US and Israeli raids by targeting all six Gulf states and Jordan. It has also attacked Gulf-owned commercial vessels.
￼
Tarek Fadlallah, chief executive of Nomura Asset Management Middle East, expects the New Delhi summit to produce a push for greater intra-Brics trade in national currencies. But, he said, India, as host, will be wary of any moves that the US could read as de-dollarisation.
“Hopes for substantive agreements are low after the foreign ministers’ meeting in May failed to produce a joint declaration for the first time,” Mr Fadlallah told The National.
Evolving world order
Brics – originally an acronym for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – has expanded since 2024 to include the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Iran, Indonesia and Ethiopia. The group says its members account for 49.5 per cent of the world’s population and about 40 per cent of global gross domestic product at purchasing power parity.
Issues that have driven Brics' evolution include greater use of local currencies, alternative payment systems, resilient supply chains and less dependence on established trade and financial networks.
China's position illustrates the complexity of the emerging order. Beijing remains Iran's largest economic lifeline, but it also has interests in the US, the Gulf and elsewhere. Analysts say China is unlikely to confront Washington directly over Iran, preferring to push for de-escalation while protecting its broader economic interests.
“For Iran, China is its biggest and basically its only paying buyer. But for China, it’s different. Iran is not its only oil supplier. It has got about 15 other suppliers. So there’s a bit of an asymmetry in that,” said Li-Chen Sim, an associate fellow at the US Middle East Institute.
“China trades many times more with the Gulf states than it actually trades with Iran. So in that sense, it’s kind of a no-brainer who it chooses in terms of trade. And on the wider trade, China also trades a lot with the US. Obviously, China wants to avoid US sanctions as well.”
The result is not necessarily the emergence of two opposing blocs, but a more fragmented system in which countries seek to maintain relationships with several centres of power at once.
That is particularly true of the Arab members of Brics, as well as India. New Delhi wants Brics to give emerging economies greater room to manoeuvre, while avoiding an alignment that would make the grouping anti-American or overly dependent on China.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to attend the summit at the weekend, his first visit to India in seven years.
The summit will follow a display of multipolar diplomacy at last week’s Shanghai Co-operation Organisation meeting, where Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mr Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin appeared together.
Washington keeps watch
Experts say the US will be monitoring developments at the Brics gathering, as it looks to improve ties with India and China but plans to increase pressure on Russia to end its war in Ukraine.
“The first thing the US will look for is to improve relations with China,” said Ms Sim. “And then, beyond that, it will look at what China can do for the US elsewhere.”
￼
This year, Mr Trump reduced tariffs on Indian goods from 50 per cent to 18 per cent, while the US and India are negotiating a trade agreement. The US President also held a meeting with Mr Xi in China in May, and Mr Xi is expected to travel to Washington after the Brics summit.
“With the Trump-Xi summit slated for Washington later this month, Beijing has no appetite for confrontation, and India has already agreed to halt Russian oil purchases in exchange for tariff relief,” said Mr Fadlallah. “Washington's hope is that this summit produces words rather than action.”
India remains heavily dependent on Russian crude, which accounted for more than 50 per cent of its crude imports in June and July and about 45 per cent in August, according to Kpler data.
For Brics, however, the challenge is whether that multipolarity can translate into collective action.
items.titleTR: US watches Brics as members juggle ties with competing powers

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Washington will watch this week’s BRICS summit through the lens of China, Russia and de-dollarization — and miss the more consequential story: Asian priorities on development, technology, energy and connectivity are quietly reshaping what BRICS has become. India has long argued for looking past BRICS’ “anti-Western” rhetoric to see how the bloc’s expansion has shifted
items.titleTR: How Asia is redefining what BRICS really means

slots.packetSpot:
The BRICS summit to be held in New Delhi on 12-13 September will test whether the group’s growing Asian weight can be turned into a common agenda. China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE are bringing issues such as energy, technology, trade, connectivity and alternative payment systems to the fore.

Nevertheless, the members do not converge on a single foreign-policy line. India is balancing its strategic ties with Washington, its commercial interests in Iran and its dependence on Russian crude oil; China, meanwhile, has broader economic ties with the United States and Gulf countries despite being Iran’s largest oil customer. The Arab members are also part of BRICS while maintaining their relations with Washington.

The Donald Trump administration’s threat of secondary sanctions against countries with financial ties to Iran makes this balance even more delicate. Although there are expectations of progress in trade in local currencies and alternative payment channels, the likelihood of concrete agreements is considered low. The resulting picture points not to a single opposing bloc, but to a fragmented order formed by members seeking to engage with multiple centres of power at the same time.
slots.packetTitle: BRICS turns toward Asia
