Ein Bericht der Zeitung Haaretz erhebt einen brisanten Vorwurf gegen Israels Premier Netanjahu: Er soll eine ausdrückliche Warnung vor einem Großangriff der Hamas eineinhalb Wochen vor dem Überfall ignoriert haben. Netanjahu dementiert - und will klagen.
￼   Ein Bericht der Zeitung Haaretz erhebt einen brisanten Vorwurf gegen Israels Premier Netanjahu: Er soll eine ausdrückliche Warnung vor einem Großangriff der Hamas eineinhalb Wochen vor dem Überfall ignoriert haben. Netanjahu dementiert - und will klagen.[mehr]
items.titleTR: Bericht über Warnung vor Hamas-Überfall: Netanjahu plant Klage

slots.packetSpot:
Haaretz wrote, based on Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval’s book “Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment”, that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed met Benjamin Netanyahu at the end of September 2023 and warned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation. According to the report, bin Zayed said this could lead to bloodshed, regional instability and damage to the Abraham Accords; Netanyahu was reportedly said to have stated that Israel was prepared for every scenario and considered an attack from the occupied West Bank more likely.

Netanyahu’s office described the claim as an “absolute lie”; it said no meeting with bin Zayed had taken place at that time and that no warning from the United Arab Emirates had reached the prime minister. It added that messages may have been exchanged through intelligence channels. The UAE Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, said it did not comment on media reports or speculation, and stated that intelligence sharing between relevant institutions takes place when necessary.

The claim intensified debate in Israel, where responsibility for 7 October is one of the main issues of the election campaign. Opposition representatives called for an investigation, holding Netanyahu responsible for failures surrounding 7 October; Netanyahu, meanwhile, rejected calls for an official government inquiry into the events.
slots.packetTitle: The disputed warning before 7 October

items.descriptionTR:
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’
Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.
items.titleTR: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief

slots.packetSpot:
Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, announced on X that his country would withdraw from the Invictus Games, held for wounded soldiers. Kainerugaba wrote that, so as not to be understood as being against King Charles III, they would not take part in any activity without the King’s approval.

Government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told the BBC that Kainerugaba decides whether the Uganda People’s Defence Forces participate in the Games and that the post reflects his current position. Uganda had recently been announced as the 26th country to take part in the Games.

The timing is being linked to a letter published at Charles’s request, stating that Harry and Meghan are no longer working members of the royal family and conduct their activities in a private capacity. According to Kainerugaba’s remarks reported by The Times, the support within some quarters of the Ministry of Defence for the “Harry-Meghan nonsense” also influenced his decision.
slots.packetTitle: Uganda’s palace line

items.descriptionTR: A Moldovan government spokesman says a flight scheduled to carry Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldova’s airspace because of a drone incursion
items.titleTR: Flight carrying Zelenskyy to Norway was delayed in Moldova because of drone incursion

slots.packetSpot:
According to Moldovan officials, a drone said to be Russian entered the country’s airspace from the direction of Ukraine, leading to the temporary closure of the airspace. At Chișinău International Airport, the plane carrying Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife Olena waited on the runway for about an hour; three departures and four arrivals were also delayed.

Officials reported that flights were permitted after it was confirmed that the drone had fallen and exploded about 160 kilometres from the airport. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the plane was nearly hit by a drone during takeoff. While a Ukrainian source speaking to AFP said the risk had been exaggerated, the Kremlin argued that there had been no threat to the plane.

Zelenskyy later arrived safely in Oslo; he attended the funeral of Norway’s King Harald V and met with Norwegian officials.
slots.packetTitle: A flight held beneath Moldova's skies

items.descriptionTR: "Remigration is nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing," said Merz on Wednesday, voicing uncharacteristically strong opposition to the far-right following a ground-shaking state election.
items.titleTR: Is German Chancellor Merz taking a harder line against the far-right after AfD win?

slots.packetSpot:
Following the AfD's landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, Friedrich Merz responded sharply to Alice Weidel's speech in the Bundestag. The German chancellor described the AfD's demand for “remigration” as synonymous with ethnic cleansing and called the party a “destructive force”; AfD lawmakers responded with protests.

Merz argued that the AfD's migration policy would severely affect the labour market. He also accused the party of contributing to Russian efforts to destabilise Germany following the thwarted drone attack on Leipzig Airport, for which Berlin holds Russia responsible.

It was announced the same day that Merz had cancelled a planned phone call with Donald Trump. His spokesperson gave no reason, said the cancellation was not due to a scheduling conflict and that no new date had been set. Trump had praised the AfD's election result. These developments suggest that Merz may be hardening his tone towards the AfD and Trump; however, it remains unclear whether this represents a lasting change of direction.
slots.packetTitle: Merz draws a line at the AfD

items.descriptionTR: ‘Guess who?’ says Fire Point, Ukrainian maker of long-range weaponry; drone alert in Moldova as Zelenskyy waited to fly out. What we know on day 1,660
items.titleTR: Ukraine war briefing: Arctic attack extends Kyiv’s strike reach into Russian gas heartland

slots.packetSpot:
Ukrainian special forces said they had targeted two natural gas facilities in the Yamalo-Nenets region, about 3,000 kilometres from the Russia-Ukraine border. One of the facilities is in Novy Urengoy, the other in the Purovsky district. The Ukrainian statement described the facilities as critical to the gas condensate sector.

Long-range weapons manufacturer Fire Point claimed that a weapon travelled more than 3,300 kilometres to strike the target; the weapon used and the extent of the damage have not been clarified. The regional governor confirmed the attack and said the damage was being assessed. According to Interfax, about 80 percent of Russia's natural gas is extracted in Yamalo-Nenets.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the impact of the attacks on the Russian economy. Ukraine also reported that it had targeted the naval base in Novorossiysk, an oil-loading terminal, military port facilities and warships carrying cruise missiles.
slots.packetTitle: The northern reach

items.descriptionTR: Korean-Japanese baseball legend Isao Harimoto, who survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima to record the most hits in Japanese baseball history, has died at the age of 86 in Tokyo.
items.titleTR: Atomic bomb survivor who became baseball legend - Harimoto dies age 86

slots.packetSpot:
According to the BBC, Isao Harimoto, Japanese baseball's all-time hits leader, died in Tokyo at the age of 86. Harimoto, the first and only player in Nippon Professional Baseball history to reach 3,000 hits, with 3,085, is also remembered for surviving at the age of five the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945.

Harimoto, who was born in Hiroshima in 1940 to Korean parents, reportedly suffered an accident as a child that caused severe burns to his right hand; he therefore threw and batted left-handed. Harimoto, who played 23 seasons for the Toei Flyers, Yomiuri Giants and Lotte Orions, ended his career in 1981 after 2,752 games, with 504 home runs, 319 stolen bases, seven batting titles and 18 all-star selections. It is stated that he contributed to the Toei Flyers' first Japan Series championship in 1962 and was inducted into the Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame in 1990.
slots.packetTitle: From Hiroshima to baseball history

items.descriptionTR:
•	Former manager says Chelsea should be stripped of title
	•	‘The title should be for the team that was second’
Mauricio Pochettino says Chelsea should be stripped of their 2016-17 Premier League title for financial rule breaches and the honour retrospectively awarded to Tottenham, who he led to second place that season.
Chelsea were fined £10m by the Football Association in July and given a suspended two-window transfer ban for multiple violations of the rules during the Roman Abramovich era. They were also fined £10.75m by the Premier League in March.
items.titleTR: Chelsea’s 2016-17 Premier League title should be given to Spurs, says Pochettino

slots.packetSpot:
Mauricio Pochettino argues that Chelsea’s 2016-17 Premier League title should be stripped because of the club’s rule breaches and awarded to second-placed Tottenham.

Chelsea, managed by Antonio Conte, finished the season seven points ahead of Pochettino’s Tottenham. Chelsea was fined £10 million by the FA and given a suspended transfer ban after admitting it had breached agent regulations linked to player transfers between 2011 and 2018 during Roman Abramovich’s era; no sporting sanction was imposed.

Pochettino argues that the two teams did not compete under the same rules. He also says his criticism is not directed at Chelsea’s players or Conte.
slots.packetTitle: Pochettino’s call for a title rewrite

items.descriptionTR:
Former NHL coach and longtime ESPN hockey analyst Barry Melrose has died.￼
Longtime hockey analyst Barry Melrose, who also coached in the NHL, has died. He was 70.
Melrose died Wednesday, his wife Cindy told ESPN’s Steve Levy.

Melrose joined ESPN in 1996. He retired from the network in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s.
“For decades, Barry Melrose was one of the most distinctive and trusted voices in hockey,” ESPN said in a statement. “His knowledge of the game was deep, his candor was refreshing, and his passion was unmistakable. He was a foundational part of ESPN’s hockey coverage, and fans and teammates truly appreciated his entertaining delivery and charismatic personality.

“We send our deepest condolences to his loved ones. He always kept it interesting and he will be missed.”
Melrose spent more than 50 years playing, coaching and analyzing hockey, including nearly 30 with ESPN.
He was the head coach of the Los Angeles Kings when the team reached the Stanley Cup Final in 1993 as Wayne Gretzky led the way.
Longtime ESPN broadcaster John Buccigross remembered Melrose in a post on X Wednesday night.
“Barry was my best friend at ESPN. A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core,” he said. “Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season.
“Chilling and fitting -- the rink was Barry’s home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever.”
Levy also paid tribute to his longtime colleague.
“For more than 30 years Barry was the unquestioned face/voice of hockey in the United States,” Levy said in a statement. “He was a man of the people, a family man, a part of my family.

“Tonight I’ll toast the kid from Kelvington who made it big but never forgot his roots. Now he can drink all the Bud Lights, smoke all the cigars and play all the rounds of golf he wants to. Barry Melrose was the best of us.”
Stories by Matt Connolly
	•	Paul Finebaum: ‘It’s getting sad’ watching Dabo Swinney at Clemson
	•	Beloved ESPN analyst, former coach dies at 70
	•	College band member dies after collapsing during Big Ten football game
	•	Big Ten basketball head coach announces he has cancer
Read the original article on MassLive. Add MassLive as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
items.titleTR: Legendary ESPN broadcaster dies at 70: ‘He will be missed’

slots.packetSpot:
According to the NHL's announcement, Barry Melrose has died at the age of 70. Melrose, who retired from ESPN in 2023 following a Parkinson's disease diagnosis, had appeared on ESPN as an ice hockey analyst since 1996.

Melrose played 300 games over six seasons in the NHL, wearing the jerseys of the Winnipeg Jets, Toronto Maple Leafs and Detroit Red Wings. In his first season as an NHL head coach, he led the Wayne Gretzky-led Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup Final. NHL commissioner Gary Bettman, Kings president Luc Robitaille and ESPN's John Buccigross shared messages emphasizing Melrose's contribution to ice hockey and its visibility in the United States.
slots.packetTitle: A life from the rink to the screen

items.descriptionTR:
In the multi-storied history of Formula 1, few moments shine with the pure unfiltered brilliance of what unfolded at the Temple of Speed on Sunday afternoon. Andrea Kimi Antonelli, the 20-year-old Italian prodigy driving for Mercedes, delivered a performance that will be etched into the sport’s folklore forever.
In the multi-storied history of Formula 1, few moments shine with the pure unfiltered brilliance of what unfolded at the Temple of Speed on Sunday afternoon. Andrea Kimi Antonelli, the 20-year-old Italian prodigy driving for Mercedes, delivered a performance that will be etched into the sport’s folklore forever.
items.titleTR: Kimi Antonelli: From the Shadows of the Grid to Immortality at Monza

slots.packetSpot:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli started his home race at Monza from 19th place and won the Italian Grand Prix. The Mercedes driver's run is being regarded as one of Formula 1's unforgettable performances; McLaren team principal Andrea Stella also described the day as iconic for Antonelli's career and for motorsport spectators.

The virtual safety car in the middle of the race changed Mercedes' tyre and strategy calculations. George Russell was leading at one stage; he said he had planned to finish the race on hard tyres and was not considering changing tyres at that point. Team principal Toto Wolff said the calculations had indicated that a one-stop strategy was the better option.

Antonelli was reported to have extended his gap over Russell in the drivers' standings to 66 points. Red Bull's Max Verstappen finished the race at Monza in third place.
slots.packetTitle: From 19th to immortality at Monza

items.descriptionTR:
Dow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second charge
A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.
The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.
items.titleTR: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role

slots.packetSpot:
A court in Hong Kong found The Wall Street Journal publisher Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia) Inc. guilty of trying to prevent or discourage former reporter Selina Cheng from standing for the leadership of the Hong Kong Journalists Association. Cheng had brought a private prosecution after losing her job in July 2024.

The court indicated that the company had required Cheng to obtain approval before standing for the association's leadership; it also recorded that the election was held outside working hours. On a separate charge alleging that Cheng was dismissed because of her union activities, Dow Jones was acquitted; the defence was said to have presented sufficient grounds to create reasonable doubt.

Dow Jones said it disagreed with the ruling and was considering its next step. The penalty will be determined later. Cheng said the case drew attention to union repression in Hong Kong, and that journalists' rights as workers are important for press freedom.
slots.packetTitle: A journalist's union rights in court in Hong Kong

items.descriptionTR: Match of the Day pundits Nedum Onuoha and Rory Smith discuss Martin Odegaard's performance in Arsenal's Champions League match against Napoli as well as his prospects for the season.
items.titleTR: Odegaard is an 'artist for this whole side' - Onuoha

items.descriptionTR: Martin Odegaard's superb strike gave Arsenal a deserved 1-0 victory over Napoli in their Champions League opener.
items.titleTR: Odegaard gives dominant Arsenal win over Napoli

slots.packetSpot:
Arsenal beat Napoli 1-0 at the Diego Armando Maradona on 9 September in the opening round of the Champions League league phase. According to Sky Sports, Martin Odegaard scored the match’s only goal at the end of a 29-pass move, firing a low shot from outside the penalty area after a one-two with Christos Tzolis.

According to the same account, Arsenal had 26 shots and reached 4.05 expected goals, but failed to take many of their chances and faced a scare late on. Odegaard was said to have had more touches than anyone else on the pitch, completed the most passes and created the most goalscoring opportunities, while Mikel Arteta described him as a decisive player who affects results. Nedum Onuoha, meanwhile, called Odegaard the team’s “artist.”
slots.packetTitle: Odegaard’s signature on Arsenal’s win

items.descriptionTR:
The Pennsylvania Democrat has already had a strained relationship with many inside his party. In the video, he spoke about working with Trump but did not outright praise him. ￼
The Pennsylvania Democrat has already had a strained relationship with many inside his party. In the video, he spoke about working with Trump but did not outright praise him.
(Image credit: Kent Nishimura)
￼
items.titleTR: Fetterman, already at odds with his party, makes surprise video for GOP convention

slots.packetSpot:
Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman’s appearance via a prerecorded video at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas became one visible example of his relationship across party lines. In the video, Fetterman introduced Republican Senator Dave McCormick, calling him “a great American,” his friend and a senator who gets things done. He also highlighted their joint work on Pennsylvania’s manufacturing industry, transportation and affordable housing.

Fetterman later said that he has been a Democrat his entire life, would continue to work with Democrats and votes in line with his party most of the time. Fetterman, who in July founded the political action committee Common Ground PA with McCormick, is reported to have drawn criticism from Democratic colleagues over positions that diverge from the party. Republican Senate members, including John Thune, were also reported to have discussed Fetterman joining the Republican Party.

In a late-August survey of registered Pennsylvania voters, 73 percent of Republicans and 22 percent of Democrats viewed Fetterman favorably. The picture shows that, despite Fetterman’s emphasis that he retains his Democratic identity, his close contact with Republican circles has drawn attention.
slots.packetTitle: Fetterman between the parties

items.descriptionTR:
The US Treasury Department announced on Wednesday it will buy back up to $6 billion of government debt as it seeks to contain long-term borrowing costs.
The move, which is triple the size of its normal operations, comes as Treasury yields have been rising in recent months, making borrowing costs higher for consumers. US Treasury yields are linked closely to Gulf states, where most currencies are directly pegged to the US dollar.
The Treasury Department previewed the action last month after long-term yields rose to near two-decade highs over fears of rising US government debt – which recently passed $40 trillion – and oil-driven inflation.
“There was like this fever that was building,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said during a Breitbart News event on Tuesday.
He said the programme was aimed to calm a "fever" in the bonds market. Long-term yields have been steadily rising since the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady in July and when traders were not convinced that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh offered a clear path to return inflation to 2 per cent.
Despite Mr Bessent’s remarks, Treasury yields rose after Wednesday’s announcement. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note rose more than 3 basis points to 4.835 per cent, while the 30-year Treasury note was up more than 2 basis points at 5.289 per cent. The two-year Treasury, which is closely linked to Federal Reserve policy moves, was trading more than two basis points higher at 4.423 per cent.
The rise in yields come amid escalating tension in the Middle East, where Iran and the US have been trading attacks on tankers in the Gulf. Oil prices rose on the attacks, with Brent crude gaining more than $2 to pass the $100-a-barrel threshold once again.
The rise in US Treasury yields also comes as the war forces some Gulf states to borrow more money to offset loss in oil revenue from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian attacks on key energy sites.
Justin Alexander, director of Khalij Economics, said during an event at the Arab Gulf States Institute that while spreads for most Gulf sovereigns over US Treasuries have either tightened or moved little during the war so far, a more prolonged conflict could lead to those spreads widening.
“That all increases the financing cost for the region at a time when countries … like Kuwait and Qatar and Bahrain, they potentially have to borrow a large amount of money. So that that does make it more expensive for Gulf companies,” Mr Alexander said during a panel session at the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington.
He also said that few Gulf states have issued debt during the war.
Saudi Arabia returned to the international debt market last week, announcing it had raised $3.25 billion during a two-tranche sukuk, while Kuwait sold $6 billion of bonds in July. Bahrain raised $1 billion through a bond issuance in June.
Mr Bessent has recently taken a more activist approach in his role, including through his intervention to support the Japanese yen. He has opposed recent criticism of the measures, including from his mentor and US investor, Stanley Druckenmiller.
"I am the house now,” Mr Bessent said on Tuesday in Texas. “And you can bet against me if you want.”
items.titleTR: Treasury triples bond buy-back programme to $6bn

slots.packetSpot:
The US Treasury Department announced that it will raise the maximum amount of government debt it can repurchase in each operation from $2 billion to $6 billion. According to the announced schedule, a repurchase operation covering securities with maturities of 10 to 20 years will be carried out on Thursday; a second operation for securities with maturities of 20 to 30 years is planned for September 24. In this second operation, the ceiling is expected to be set at no less than $4 billion.

The move comes at a time when government bond yields are rising and pressure on borrowing costs is increasing. On Wednesday, the yield on the 30-year US Treasury bond exceeded 5.3%, while the 10-year bond yield rose above 4.84%. Since the start of the year, 10- and 30-year yields have reportedly risen by around 70 and 45 basis points, respectively.

Persistent inflation, economic uncertainty linked to the Iran war and rising public debt are cited among the factors behind the pressure in the bond market. The US national debt reportedly exceeded $40 trillion last month. The Treasury's repurchase move is presented as an effort to lower yields; its effect on yields, however, remains uncertain.
slots.packetTitle: The Treasury moves against the yield tide

items.descriptionTR: LIV Golf, the professional men's golf tour owned by the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection as it begins restructuring, the organization announced on Tuesday.
items.titleTR: LIV Golf could soon be majority player-owned as organization files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy

slots.packetSpot:
LIV Golf's Chapter 11 filing in the United States has deepened uncertainty over the league's future following the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund's decision to withdraw its support. Chief executive Scott O'Neil said the league aims to move to a player-focused ownership model while continuing operations and to emerge from the bankruptcy process in early 2027. However, debts owed to star players and the question of whether it can retain its roster and the scale of its tournaments remain unresolved.

This uncertainty has also placed event and infrastructure plans in South Australia at the centre of political debate. The Peter Malinauskas government had extended LIV Golf's hosting in the state until 2031; it had announced a $45 million renovation plan linked to its move to North Adelaide Golf Course in 2028. The project, which will involve the loss of 585 trees, will serve not only LIV Golf but also public use outside events, according to the government's account. The government has also secured the right to host the Australian Open from 2028.

The opposition and some commentators say the bankruptcy filing has heightened questions over the rationale for this investment. The government, meanwhile, argues that taxpayers are not exposed to LIV Golf's financial difficulties. If LIV Golf can emerge from its current difficulties, the status of the advance payment expected by the club for the tournament scheduled to be held at Adelaide's Kooyonga Golf Club in March 2027 remains uncertain.
slots.packetTitle: LIV Golf's uncertain future reaches South Australia

items.descriptionTR: The European Central Bank increased interest rates for the second time since the Iran war started, responding to signs inflation is set to stay well above 2%. The deposit rate was lifted by a quarter-point to 2.5%. Bloomberg's Oliver Crook reports from Berlin. (Source: Bloomberg)
items.titleTR: ECB Hikes Interest Rates for Second Time Since Iran War

slots.packetSpot:
The European Central Bank raised its key deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%. Against a backdrop in which the conflict in the Middle East is complicating the inflation outlook through energy prices, the ECB pointed to upside risks for inflation and downside risks for growth. Inflation in the euro area reportedly reached 3.3% in August, while energy inflation reached 14.3%.

According to Christine Lagarde, the conflict in the Middle East and developments in Russia's war in Ukraine could keep headline inflation above the ECB's 2% target for a long time. Core inflation excluding energy and food is projected to be 2.5% in 2026, 2.6% in 2027 and 2.3% in 2028. The direction of subsequent rate moves remains uncertain; some market strategists expect further increases.
slots.packetTitle: Energy uncertainty shadows the ECB's rate decision

items.descriptionTR: [RFI] Mali's warring sides are increasingly using artificial intelligence to fight an information war alongside their battle on the ground, a study published Wednesday has found. Jihadists are experimenting with relatively basic AI propaganda, separatist networks are creating fake online characters and Russia's Africa Corps is using the technology on a far more sophisticated scale.
items.titleTR: Mali: AI Deepfakes and Fake Fighters Reshape Mali's Information War

slots.packetSpot:
Research published on Wednesday by the Dakar-based Timbuktu Institute finds that generative artificial intelligence has added a new layer to the conflict in Mali at the level of information warfare. According to the research, while the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM is experimenting with relatively basic AI propaganda, supporter networks around the FLA are creating artificial online characters to spread their messages. One example identified by the researchers is the Tuareg fighter “Azzghim,” who harshly criticises Russia’s Africa Corps; this character is said to have been generated by AI.

The research assesses that Mali’s transitional administration and Africa Corps are using generative AI in a state-level, professionalised and systematic manner. Artificial videos, anti-Western deepfakes and generated social-media comments are listed among these methods. According to Bakary Sambe, 19 Russian disinformation campaigns have been recorded in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger since 2018; some content identified by the Timbuktu Institute reached around five million views. Content circulated after the 25 April clashes in Kidal is reported to have aimed to portray Africa Corps positively; it is also reported to have spread claims that France and Ukraine support JNIM and FLA attackers.

Sambe says AI has not created the existing divisions in Mali, but has amplified them. A warning is made that automated translation and personalised messages could increase armed groups’ capacity for propaganda and recruitment. Military uses such as target identification and drone operations are treated in the research largely as a future possibility; it is stated that this capability could be a serious force multiplier for armed groups.
slots.packetTitle: AI opens a new front in Mali’s war

items.descriptionTR: French President Emmanuel Macron is hosting dozens of leaders, technology experts and scientists in Paris for a two-day global space summit that opens on Wednesday, as major US companies including SpaceX and Blue Origin stay away.
items.titleTR: Macron hosts global space summit in Paris snubbed by US companies

items.descriptionTR:
A two-day international space summit organised in Paris began on Wednesday amid French-Emirati efforts to strengthen industry ties and develop low Earth orbit technologies.
UAE astronaut Sultan Al Neyadi, who is also the Minister of State for Youth Affairs, is representing his country at the summit, which has been organised by France and Germany. It is focused on strengthening investments in the space industry and launching a global discussion on governing space.
More than 90 countries are represented at the summit, but US technology companies withdrew following pressure from the White House, which views the event as too pro-European. Germany is represented by its Minister for Research, Technology and Space, Dorothee Bar.
"We will have a series of opportunities, common investments, common programmes and partnerships to strengthen, obviously, the European space industry and space research, but also partnerships with a lot of other countries," French President Emmanuel Macron said in his opening statement at the Grand Palais in Paris.
The Emirati defence company Edge signed a deal with Munich's The Exploration Company to work towards a sea-based launch system based in the UAE. Edge subsidiary Fada also said it would collaborate with France’s Infinite Orbits to roll out Space Situational Awareness surveillance capacities in low Earth orbit.
￼
“This Franco-Emirati collaboration illustrates the two companies' shared commitment to strengthening space surveillance capabilities while consolidating industrial ties between the French and UAE space ecosystems,” the Elysee said in a document listing more than 50 new business agreements agreed at the summit.
AI satellites
Abu Dhabi start-up Tactica AI signed a separate deal with France’s Safran to deepen co-operation in space data analysis. Additionally, Marlan Space, a subsidiary of the Abu Dhabi global investment firm Marlan Holding, and Loft Orbital, which has its headquarters in the US and a French chief executive, said they would work with France’s Mistral AI to develop a constellation of 50 satellites equipped with on-board AI.
Led by Marlan Space, the consortium will mobilise $1 billion in investments in France. The project will involve the US space-based intelligence company BlackSky, and illustrates the joint French and Emirati ambition to become world leaders in AI in space, the Elysee said.
“The initial applications, developed using Loft Orbital’s space platform and Mistral AI’s artificial intelligence models, will focus notably on fire detection, protecting populations against ballistic threats, and securing critical energy infrastructure,” it said. Earlier this week, an 80 per cent stake in Marlan Holding was acquired by Abu Dhabi’s International Holding Company amid growth in the global space economy.
In a further signal of tight UAE-French relations in the space industry, Hamdullah Mohib, acting chief executive of the satellite company Orbitworks, was among a dozen international chief executives who held a closed-door round-table meeting with Mr Macron ahead of the summit's launch on Wednesday. Orbitworks is a joint venture between Marlan Space and Loft Orbital.
￼
Last month, Orbitworks signed a deal with France in one of the first instances of a European government space agency becoming a customer of a satellite constellation owned and built in the Middle East. Orbitworks also shipped the Altair-1 satellite to the US for a launch with SpaceX in October.
International co-operation
Dr Al Neyadi, who is among a UAE delegation that also included Space Agency chairman and Sports Minister Dr Ahmad Al Falasi, is the only Arab astronaut attending the summit, highlighting the Emirates' rising profile in the sector.
Speaking alongside a panel of international astronauts, Dr Al Neyadi said the rapid growth of the UAE's two-decade-old space programme was rooted in international co-operation. "We’re open to any sort of collaboration and international deals in a way to push this with the capability of knowledge transfer as well," he said. He pointed to past partnerships with Russia, the US, Japan and South Korea.
In 2023, Dr Al Neyadi spent six months on the International Space Station and became the first Arab astronaut to perform a spacewalk. He has become a champion for the UAE's space programme and its astronauts.
In June, he and astronaut Hazza Al Mansouri completed Nasa's geology training in New Mexico, as the UAE's space programme prepares for new destinations, such as the Moon.
Around 20 astronauts are attending the summit, most of them from Western countries. Italy has the largest contingent with three astronauts: Samantha Cristoforetti, Luca Parmitano and Andrea Patassa.
Despite Mr Macron's ambition to strengthen the European space industry, divisions within the continent have led to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni staying away.
France has led calls for Europe to increase its autonomy in space, while Germany appears less willing to close the door on SpaceX, which dominates the modern launch market. China, India and Japan are participating in the summit, as are leaders from Vietnam and South Korea.
items.titleTR: Space summit begins as France and UAE intensify efforts to develop low Earth orbit technology

slots.packetSpot:
The two-day global space summit that opened in Paris began with industrial partnerships and investment plans between France and the UAE. Space governance, space traffic, the sharing of scientific data and Europe’s position in space are on the agenda at the meeting opened by Emmanuel Macron.

At the summit, attended by UAE astronaut and Minister of State for Youth Affairs Sultan Al Neyadi, Edge and Munich-based The Exploration Company announced an agreement to develop a sea-launch system in the UAE. Edge subsidiary Fada reportedly entered into cooperation with France’s Infinite Orbits for surveillance capacity in low Earth orbit, while Abu Dhabi-based Tactica AI reportedly partnered with Safran for space data analysis.

Marlan Space, Loft Orbital and Mistral AI plan to develop a constellation of 50 AI-equipped satellites, which BlackSky will also join. The consortium led by Marlan Space is expected to mobilise $1 billion in investment in France. The Exploration Company, meanwhile, announced that it had raised €387 million for the development of its reusable Nyx capsule, bringing its total capital to around €577 million.

Major US space companies, including SpaceX and Blue Origin, are not attending the summit. According to Politico, citing three anonymous sources familiar with the talks, a White House official told companies that participation could be seen as implicit support for EU policy positions; the White House did not immediately respond to AFP’s request for comment. The absence comes amid ongoing debate over Europe’s dependence on the US and its own launch capacity.
slots.packetTitle: New partnerships in space take shape in Paris

items.descriptionTR: Drinking this year's champagne might give you a heftier headache as France's record heatwaves are forcing some producers to up the alcohol levels, industry officials said Wednesday.
items.titleTR: Heat forces French champagne makers to stiffen their drink

slots.packetSpot:
Record heatwaves and drought in France are reportedly accelerating sugar accumulation in Champagne grapes. This year, the harvest began as early as 6 August and became widespread on 17 August; according to the Comité Champagne, this was a schedule two weeks earlier than in 2025.

French authorities allowed some Champagne houses to produce sparkling wine with an alcohol content of up to 15%. It was stated that the permission granted for this level, normally capped at 13%, would concern only a small number of producers, while the post-harvest average remained below 12%.

While the Comité Champagne said the crop had the potential to yield great, even exceptional wines, co-chair Maxime Toubart stated that such early harvests could become commonplace within 10 to 15 years. According to the agriculture minister's assessment, the nationwide wine harvest in 2026 could be the lowest in the past 70 years because of heat, drought and wildfires; Champagne production could also fall 50% below normal.
slots.packetTitle: Heat's mark on Champagne

items.descriptionTR:
Fourteen men have gone on trial in Paris on smuggling charges related to the drowning of more ⁠than 30 people five years ago, the worst disaster on record involving migrants in the English Channel.
The people died after their overloaded dinghy deflated as they made the perilous crossing from France to the UK, across one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
Investigators ⁠allege that Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks organised the migrants' passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. ⁠The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter, ‌facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.
A French fishing vessel alerted emergency services after spotting bodies floating in the waters off the French coast near Calais in November 2021, according to the court referral order. Twenty-seven victims were recovered, while at least four others were never found. Only two men survived.
The victims were mainly Iraqi Kurds, but also included Afghans, Ethiopians, an Egyptian, a Somali, an Iranian Kurd and a Vietnamese national. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl.
￼
The migrants had been packed on to a flimsy dinghy that was non-certified and unfit for open-sea navigation, and was not equipped with enough life jackets, the court document showed. Experts concluded its occupants had “no chance” of effectively dealing with an emergency at sea.
Among the defendants facing involuntary manslaughter charges are alleged organisers, transporters and logistics co-ordinators connected to the smuggling groups. Prosecutors argue their actions helped create the conditions that led to the disaster, even if some were not physically present when the boat launched.
Two defendants' lawyers said their clients could not be held responsible for the deaths as they played minor roles in the chain of events.
Lawyer Marie Guegot's client is accused of manslaughter for having housed one of ‌the victims before they took the boat.
“For ⁠him, he was hosting a friend from his village in Afghanistan. We don’t have those responsible, the heads of the network, here,” she said.
￼
Deaths were 'avoidable'
Two ‌of the defendants have eluded French authorities and will be tried in absentia.
A British inquiry into the disaster found the deaths ⁠were avoidable. It concluded that a French naval vessel failed to respond to a call for help from the ⁠British coastguard, which in turn made “a number of flawed decisions”, including ending a search for survivors too early.
Members of the French military are currently under formal investigation for failing to help the migrants when they were in danger.
“This is the first step of the legal process with this trial that concerns the smugglers. And the next step will be the trial, hopefully, for the marines,” said Thomas Ricard, one of the lawyers for the victims' families.
Nine people who came from Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan, were due to testify at the trial, Mr Ricard added. “That will allow them some recovery as part of this long process of grief.”
The trial is expected to end on September 30.
items.titleTR: Fourteen suspected migrant smugglers go on trial in Paris over mass drowning in Channel

slots.packetSpot:
More than 30 people died in November 2021 when a boat described as overloaded and unfit for open-sea navigation deflated while attempting to cross from northern France to the United Kingdom. In the trial that has begun in Paris, 14 people alleged to be linked to Afghan and Iraqi Kurdish smuggling networks are being tried on charges of involuntary manslaughter, organised assistance with illegal migration and criminal conspiracy. Two of the defendants will be tried in absentia.

The bodies of 27 people were found, while at least four are reported still missing; two men survived. Most of the victims were Iraqi Kurds; they also included Afghans, Ethiopians, an Egyptian, a Somali, an Iranian Kurd and a Vietnamese person. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl.

Prosecutors argue that organisers, transporters and logistics coordinators contributed to the creation of the conditions that led to the disaster. Some defence lawyers, however, argue that their clients played minor roles in the chain of events and cannot be held responsible for the deaths. A United Kingdom inquiry concluded that the deaths were preventable; it criticised a French navy vessel's response to the distress call and the UK coastguard's early termination of the search. A formal investigation into French military personnel is continuing over allegations that they failed to assist people in danger. The trial is expected to end on 30 September.
slots.packetTitle: The Channel disaster's first criminal trial

items.descriptionTR: Aerial footage shows a sinkhole where Nicolas Cage's Malibu driveway stood after coastal erosion from Hurricane Marie remnants triggered a gas leak and road closure.
items.titleTR: Massive sinkhole opens outside Nicolas Cage’s Malibu mansion

slots.packetSpot:
A large sinkhole opened Tuesday morning where the driveway of a beachfront property in Malibu had been. Coastal erosion is reported to have accelerated following storm surges and high tides linked to the remnants of Hurricane Marie.

The collapse reportedly caused a gas leak shortly before 6:00 a.m. SoCalGas crews brought the leak under control hours later; gas service was shut off along an 85-foot section of the street as a precaution. Malibu officials blocked access to five homes on the road while engineers assessed the damage.

Entertainment media report that the property belongs to Nicolas Cage. According to records cited by The New York Times, Cage bought the property in 2024; his representatives did not comment.
slots.packetTitle: Ground gives way on the Malibu coast

items.descriptionTR:
Witness testimonies, videos, pictures and other evidence provided by former senior officials of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) have corroborated earlier reports that the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) used chemical weapons in attacks between 2024 and 2025.
Speaking to Euronews, the former officials added their voices to an existing trove of evidence reported by The New York Times and The Washington Post.
The OPCW former officials spoke to eight witnesses in Nairobi, Kenya, where thousands of Sudanese refugees had fled to escape the continuing war. They said witnesses were able to provide "a number of credible incidents involving unexplained illness following military activity".
The individuals spoken to were themselves involved in emergency response, had treated victims of the attacks or were directly exposed to the chemical weapons, the report said.
Most significantly, two witnesses described an attack at the Al Jili Oil Refinery in the Sudanese capital Khartoum, which was then under control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), against whom the SAF was fighting.
They described "barrel-shaped objects" overhead, "unfamiliar odours" and strange emissions and explosives, as well as "acute respiratory symptoms" and changes to vegetation nearby.
The former officials called on the OPCW to launch an investigation. The SAF has continuously denied using chemical weapons.
The war erupted in April 2023 during a power struggle between the SAF and RSF. Sanctioned SAF leader Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan has vowed to continue fighting until the RSF is defeated, rejecting repeated attempts by the US and regional powers to broker a ceasefire. Both forces have been accused of grave abuses.
The US had initially held the SAF responsible for carrying out chlorine gas attacks in 2024, issuing sanctions on the SAF-aligned government as a result.
The New York Times and Washington Post reports revealed the SAF has not only used chemical weapons in the devastating war but also built a secret stockpile that it later attempted to conceal and carried out bomb tests in Sudan's desert.
A Sudanese coalition on Monday called on the UN Human Rights Council to identify and publicly name the countries and external entities supporting the SAF and to renew the mandate of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan.
The SAF is also believed to be collaborating with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to smuggle weapons components. Last September, Moammar Al Eryani, Yemen’s Minister of Information, accused the Iran-backed militia of manufacturing chemical weapons from smuggled components. He said that his assessment was based on recent intelligence from several sources, marking the first direct accusation of its kind from a Yemeni government official.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced millions and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises, with an estimated 20 million people suffering from hunger.
items.titleTR: Former watchdog officials further reveal Sudan Armed Forces' use of chemical weapons

slots.packetSpot:
A 32-page review conducted by former senior officials of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) suggests that certain cases seen following military activity in Sudan in 2024 and 2025 may indicate possible chemical weapons use. Accounts from eight Sudanese witnesses interviewed in Nairobi describe respiratory and eye complaints, unusual smells, coloured emissions mixing into the air, unexplained illnesses and environmental changes. The witnesses include people who say they were directly exposed, emergency responders, a healthcare worker who treated affected patients, and people who provided documents or digital material.

Two witnesses who separately described an incident at the El Cili Oil Refinery near Khartoum in September 2024 said a military aircraft passed overhead immediately before it, that they saw barrel-shaped objects, and that unusual emissions and smells emerged. Their accounts also said that around 20 workers in an area then controlled by the Rapid Support Forces developed respiratory symptoms, and that vegetation near the scene later changed. Experts say the symptoms are consistent with exposure to an airborne irritant or hazardous chemical, but that the substance could not be identified and that chemical weapons use could not be conclusively confirmed.

Images in the review were seen by Euronews; however, the witnesses were not interviewed directly, and the video and other digital material could not be examined. The former officials are calling on the OPCW and states parties to open an investigation based on the preliminary findings. In early September, The New York Times and The Washington Post also published investigations based on Middle Eastern intelligence; the United States imposed sanctions on Sudan in April 2025 over allegations of chemical weapons use. The Sudanese government has repeatedly denied the accusations; it did not respond to Euronews' request for comment before publication.

In the war that began in 2023, around 14 million people have been displaced, according to UN data from April 2026. Around 19.5 million people are also facing acute food insecurity and famine conditions.
slots.packetTitle: Calls for an inquiry into chemical weapons allegations in Sudan

items.descriptionTR: Alexander Zverev ‌took another big step towards a second Grand Slam ‌title by beating Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp 6-2 7-5 6-1 to reach the US Open semi-finals.
items.titleTR: Zverev's US Open rocky road turns into smooth sailing to the semi-finals

slots.packetSpot: Alexander Zverev reached the US Open semi-finals by beating Botic van de Zandschulp 6-2, 7-5 and 6-1 in the night session at Arthur Ashe Stadium. Zverev said he watched Ben Shelton's match, in which Shelton beat defending champion Carlos Alcaraz, until 3.30 a.m. He will face Karen Khachanov in the semi-finals, after Khachanov advanced when Alexander Blockx withdrew because of injury.
slots.packetTitle: A night watch into the semi-finals

items.descriptionTR: IAEA chief Grossi told the Board of Governors that Tehran had provided no information on declared nuclear materials and inspectors had no on-site access, as Iran's parliament speaker threatened US energy assets with retaliatory strikes and the IRGC warned vessels off the southern Hormuz corridor.
items.titleTR: IAEA says Iran blocking nuclear inspectors as Hormuz threats mount

slots.packetSpot:
The IAEA Board of Governors referred the matter to the UN Security Council because Iran had failed to provide information on previously declared nuclear material and to grant access to the facilities needed for verification. According to the agency, key facilities including Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan have been inaccessible since the US-Israel war that began in June 2025.

Iran's UN representative in Vienna, Reza Najafi, described the decision as baseless and politically motivated; he said ongoing military operations and security conditions were preventing inspector access, but that Tehran had nevertheless not suspended its safeguards obligations. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi also accused the US and its European partners of using the disruption in the verification process itself as grounds for the decision.

Following the referral backed by the US, France, Germany and the United Kingdom, Russia and China are expected to oppose or block additional steps at the Security Council. As Donald Trump renewed his threat to target the Pickaxe Mountain facilities near Natanz, Director General Rafael Grossi said there was no evidence that Iran was systematically moving towards developing nuclear weapons. The IAEA suspects that Iran has around 400 kilograms of highly enriched uranium; it is stated that, if further enriched, this amount could theoretically be used to produce ten nuclear weapons.
slots.packetTitle: Where oversight ends

items.descriptionTR: Rwanda forward Joy-Lance Mickels has helped Azerbaijan's Sabah reach the Champions League proper on their competition debut, and is now looking to down the team he supports.
items.titleTR: The Rwandan eyeing Champions League history against Man Utd

items.descriptionTR:
As Manchester United were playing their first pre-season friendly of the season in Helsinki in July, Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK were preparing to play their fourth competitive Uefa Champions League qualifier of the season, just north of the Finnish capital.
United lost their friendly 1-0 to Wrexham on July 18. Ten days later, Sabah defeated Finnish champions KuPS 2-0, sealing a 3-0 aggregate win.
Sabah were expected to be eliminated in the qualifying stages, but they carried on winning, advancing through four rounds. Their reward is a trip to Old Trafford on Thursday, where Manchester United will play against an Azerbaijani team for the first time in their history.
For United, it’s a first Champions League game since 2023 – an unexpected absence for one of the biggest clubs in the world. First, they were relegated to the Europa League, losing the 2025 final. Then no European football at all last season.
Uefa, Europe's governing body, missed United and their huge popularity from their various club competitions. It was no surprise 80 per cent of the crowd in Gothenburg, Sweden, supported United over current champions of Europe Paris Saint-Germain during their friendly last month. But appeal alone isn’t enough. United need success on the pitch.
United, the first English club to play in the European Cup in the 1950s, also need the revenue that continental football brings – and on a regular basis.
Missing out on broadcast, commercial and ticket revenue meant United went from being one of the most profitable clubs in the world to a loss-making one. As their finances floundered amid poor recruitment, new decision-makers, led by Ineos, needed to cut costs and scale back their spending. United, once the biggest payers for talent, are now living within their means, which admittedly are still substantial.
Few are expecting United to win a fourth European Cup this season. Most are expecting them to qualify from the group stage along with 23 other teams – eight automatic, 16 who enter a play-off – from the 36 qualified clubs.
It will be a first for United under the new format – a fail-safe to protect the strongest clubs and to guarantee at least eight matches and increased revenue.
United are one of five English and five Spanish clubs in the competition and need a win on Thursday after a faltering start to the Premier League season in which they have won one, drawn one and lost one.
United have conceded twice in each of their three games, including in the final minute of added time at Everton on Sunday, a 2-2 draw after Michael Carrick’s side had led twice.
The opening game of the season saw the worst result, a 2-0 defeat at promoted Hull City, before they beat another promoted side, Ipswich Town, 5-2. Manchester City, who have won all three domestic games so far, are the next league visitors in Sunday’s Manchester derby.
A Thursday night fixture leaves United with 48 hours less to prepare for the derby than their opponents. This season is set to be significantly different from last term, when United played only 40 games. It will likely be closer to 60 this time around.
United needed a bigger squad, and brought in three midfielders to replace Casemiro and the injured Manuel Ugarte. Their most recent recruit – Carlos Baleba – is recovering from injury as he hopes to start his United career soon.
Carrick likes to stick with his strongest squad but knows it is important to rotate this season. There are likely to be changes against Sabah, who, like Grimsby Town a year ago, have little to lose. It’s a rare chance for fans to get tickets at a venue which is sold out for every game, a night under the lights, and a chance to hear what has become an unfamiliar sound: the Champions League anthem.
The boss is already looking ahead to Thursday's Champions League encounter 👊 pic.twitter.com/33y6NbI2KP
— Manchester United (@ManUtd) September 6, 2026
United were at a low point following a 15th-place league finish in the 2024/25 season and a defeat in the Europa League final. The club are slowly but surely rising again, with sensible recruitment and a clear plan to make the club great again.
Those who have watched United so far this season are likely to be a little more circumspect. Thursday brings a chance to boost confidence and start a huge competition on the right note.
For United's opponents, Sabah, it is a huge step. The club was only formed in 2017 and didn’t win a trophy until 2025, the Azerbaijani Cup, which was followed up by last season’s league-and-cup double.
Players from 16 countries, including Nigeria, South Africa, Algeria and Rwanda in Africa, to the Balkans and even Jamaica, Guadeloupe and Curacao in the Caribbean, represent Sabah.
They are managed by Valdas Dambrauskas, a 49-year-old Lithuanian who moved to London in 2002, aged 25, to study to be a coach. The move was funded by prize money from the Lithuanian version of TV programme Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, which was equivalent to six months’ salary in Lithuania.
What a story. From soccer schools to coach of an opposition team.
John Shiels on Sabah coach Valdas Dambrauskas
Dambrauskas volunteered as a coach and took several jobs to support his ambitions. He also coached with Man United’s Soccer Schools for five years after John Shiels, who headed United’s charitable foundation, gave him a chance. Dambrauskas said this week that he will be forever grateful to Shiels for the opportunity.
“I’ve been following him for years and watched his journey,” Shiels told The National. “What a story. From soccer schools to coach of an opposition team. Good habits and behaviours formed with the Soccer Schools in those days.”
Sabah is the 10th club of Dambrauskas’ career so far, and he has won 13 trophies across five countries.
Based in a town of 20,000 close to the capital, Baku, Sabah are the lowest-ranked team in the competition and will play Champions League football for the first time.
They progressed through four qualifying rounds against Welsh side TNS, Finland’s KuPS and Aarhus of Denmark, against whom they scored four goals in 30 minutes to turn the tie around in the second leg.
A more dramatic ending followed in the next play-off round against Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva. Hapoel won the first leg 2-1 at home in front of just 1,048 fans and were leading 4-2 on aggregate with 16 minutes to play in the second leg.
That 28,000 people were in attendance for the return game shows the interest for football in Azerbaijan, and they were delighted as a Sabah goal in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the game into extra time, where they won 5-2 and 6-4 on aggregate.
They now get to take on United, plus other giants including Arsenal, Barcelona, Borussia Dortmund, Villarreal and Napoli.
items.titleTR: Manchester United cautiously optimistic as Champions League football returns to Old Trafford

slots.packetSpot:
The Champions League match at Old Trafford will be Manchester United's first return since 2023; for Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK, founded in 2017, it will be their first experience of the competition's league phase. Sabah came through four qualifying rounds by beating KuPS, TNS, Aarhus and Hapoel Beer-Sheva; they will take the field as the lowest-ranked team in the match expected to be played at 20:00 BST on Thursday.

Manchester United have started the league under Michael Carrick with one win, one draw and one defeat; they conceded two goals in each of the three matches. Sabah's 32-year-old Rwandan Joy-Lance Mickels, a United supporter since childhood, is expected to start. Mickels, who scored four goals in the qualifiers, is set to become the first Rwandan footballer to play in the Champions League proper.

Tonight also marks a personal return for Dambrauskas: the Lithuanian coach worked for five years at Manchester United Soccer Schools. While Sabah are expected to play some home matches at Baku Olympic Stadium because their ground does not meet UEFA requirements, their fixture list also includes Arsenal, Barcelona, Borussia Dortmund, Villarreal and Napoli.
slots.packetTitle: Two beginnings at Old Trafford

items.descriptionTR: [Dabanga] Amsterdam -- Humanitarian funding crisis is forcing patients to travel further for treatment as remaining hospitals struggle to absorb the growing demand, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns international aid cuts are forcing clinics across Sudan to close, leaving people to make longer and more dangerous journeys for healthcare and pushing the country's remaining hospitals towards breaking point.
items.titleTR: Sudan: Sudanese Clinics Close Amid Aid Cuts, Leaving Millions With Shrinking Access to Healthcare - MSF

slots.packetSpot:
According to Médecins Sans Frontières' warning, international humanitarian aid cuts are leading to clinic closures and a weakening of health services in Sudan. The organisation says that in a country where war and the humanitarian crisis continue, patients are having to travel longer distances, while demand is shifting to the hospitals that remain operational.

According to MSF data, admissions to facilities it supports in Zalingei and Rokero in Central Darfur rose by 22.5 percent in January-April 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. In May, 45 primary health centres in the region were no longer able to receive support after the organisation funding them ran out of money.

After a humanitarian organisation left Tanedba camp in El Gedaref state in June, maternity and surgical services closed; MSF says it has taken over the emergency department until the end of 2026. According to the organisation, pregnant women requiring caesarean sections may have to make journeys of up to three hours to reach the nearest town. The number of aid organisations operating around Um Rakuba camp has also fallen from about 35 in 2021 to fewer than 10.

After support was cut at Hamidiya displacement camp, daily patient visits reportedly fell from about 200 to 40 and vaccination stopped. MSF reports that it operates the only 200-bed hospital in Tawila; cases of malaria and malnutrition are increasing ahead of the peak of the rainy season.

According to UN data cited by MSF, the $2.87 billion response plan is 41 percent funded, and about 37 percent of health facilities in Sudan are completely out of service. The organisation also notes that the OECD's announced 13.8 percent decline in aid from EU institutions and 35.8 percent decline in global humanitarian aid for 2025 do not mean equivalent cuts for Sudan; some European donors have maintained or increased their support.
slots.packetTitle: The burden on the hospitals left standing

items.descriptionTR:
The on-court connection between Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese sparked brighter than any other on a pre-dawn tip-off in the U.S. 
Team USA left nothing to chance in its 34th consecutive World Cup victory on Thursday in Berlin, Germany. The rout was over nearly as soon as it began in a suffocating 108-56 win over Hungary to reach the semifinals and continue the quest for a fifth consecutive World Cup gold.
The U.S. will face the winner of Spain vs. Australia, the final game of the quarterfinals to be played on Thursday. Matchups between China and France, and Belgium and Germany, are on the other side of the bracket. 
The record-shattering win took the same path as those before it in this tournament. Head coach Kara Lawson rolled out her veterans to start, and finished with the young, up-and-coming crew to boost the lead further. The 108 points were the most by a team in a quarterfinal game in World Cup history, and tied for second-most in a knockout game at the World Cup. 
More unreal stats are below, as well as takeaways from Team USA’s statement victory. 
Caitlin Clark-Angel Reese connection thriving
The on-court connection between Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese sparked brighter than any other on a pre-dawn tip-off in the U.S. 
Clark found Reese three times in about five minutes for buckets in the second quarter that helped pad the lead. And in the second half, Reese returned the favor, assisting Clark on a bucket off the steal. 
Angel Reese with another steal, and return of favor to CC 🙌#FIBAWWCpic.twitter.com/Hl4Eei5XB0
— FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup (@FIBAWWC) September 10, 2026
“We’ve played against each other so many times, so I’m sure we know each other’s game like the back of each other’s hands,” Reese said on the post-game broadcast interview. “It’s fun. We just continue to build chemistry because we know we’re going to be USA teammates for a while.” 
Clark’s version of Team USA is a highly successful (and incredibly fun to watch) run-and-gun offense that Reese fits into well. She can run the floor and is shooting more efficiently, entering the game at 57.1% through three games. The chemistry blossoming between different iterations of Clark, Reese, Paige Bueckers and Aliyah Boston will be the future, potentially as soon as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. 
Clark scored 10 points in a game-high 20 minutes. She had 9 assists, 3 rebounds, 2 steals and 3 turnovers. Reese scored nine, shooting 80% (4-5) with 6 rebounds, 3 assists, 2 steals, 1 block and 2 turnovers. 
Unreal numbers
The stats for the U.S. were gaudy. 
Their 31 assists were the most in a quarterfinal game, and the U.S. did it on 40 made baskets. No matter the lineup on the floor, the ball moved multiple times to a more wide-open shooter. They shot 59% from the floor, consisting of 52% inside the arc and 52% from outside it. The team went 12 of 23 from the perimeter, led by Rhyne Howard (3 of 5), Kahleah Copper (2 of 2), Chelsea Gray (2 of 2) and Boston (2 of 3). 
The 108 points scored tied the second-most in a knockout game with the 1986 U.S. team that defeated the Soviet Union in the final. The U.S. holds the top five spots behind Brazil’s total of 110 points over the U.S. in the 1994 semifinals. Every player scored, and five were in double digits. Howard scored 15, while Copper and Jackie Young chipped in 10 apiece. 
The 59-30 halftime lead marked a record for first-half point totals in a quarterfinal, while Team USA’s 59 points were its best after 20 minutes of any knockout game at the World Cup. The 29-point margin at the half was the largest of any previous World Cup quarterfinal game. 
The final winning margin blew out that of France over Hungary. The French are favored to give the U.S. a run for the title, and moved up into the No. 1 spot in the Women’s World Cup power rankings after the U.S. narrowly escaped Italy in the group stage. 
Napheesa Collier’s turn to break out 
Collier played the role of pace car for Team USA. She scored 10 points in the first quarter to spell a 36-12 lead and finished with a team-high 19, shooting 69% with 6 rebounds and 1 block. 
Business-like performance from Phee 🔥  🇺🇸 #USABWNT x #FIBAWWC 🏆 pic.twitter.com/ZgwMHIXYkt
— USA Basketball (@usabasketball) September 10, 2026
Collier subbed out at the first mark for Boston, but quickly returned and ran up the score in a lineup with Boston, Clark, Young and Paige Bueckers. She took advantage of attention on Boston in the paint, hitting open layups, and utilized feeds from Clark. She and Breanna Stewart have thrived with the younger group. 
The WNBA MVP runner-up only returned to 5-on-5 action in July after surgeries on both of her ankles. The World Cup is serving as a ramp-up to peak in the WNBA playoffs and potentially lead the Lynx to a record fifth WNBA championship. 
No A’ja, no (paint) problem
Heading to Germany without four-time WNBA MVP A’ja Wilson was a loss, but not one the U.S. couldn’t absorb. There is no nation deeper in talent, and Team USA showcased it with a suffocating paint presence against Hungary’s frontcourt tandem of Dorka Juhasz and Virag Takacs-Kiss. 
The U.S. led in paint points, 20-0, at one point and finished the half leading 32-4. They scored more in the paint than Hungary did as they built a 59-30 halftime lead. By game’s end, it was up to 52-16. The U.S. won the boards, 49-29.
Juhasz and Takacs-Kiss were each held to two points apiece and 12 combined rebounds, sharply below their three-game World Cup averages. Juhasz averaged 15.3 points, shooting 50% and a third-best 15.2 rebounds per game. She was 1 of 12 against Team USA, and her Lynx teammate, Collier. Takacs-Kiss averaged 14 points and 13.7 rebounds per game, fifth in the tournament. 
It left Hungary to 28 3-point attempts, of which they made 9. Reka Lelik led Hungary with 12 points. Agnes Torok scored 11. 

Will Lawson ever tweak the starting lineup? 
The quarterfinal against an overmatched Hungary team presented the perfect opportunity for Lawson to tweak the starting lineup. That she didn’t indicates she won’t at all through the rest of this tournament. 
The lineup at tip remained the national team veterans: Gray, Young, Copper, Collier and Stewart. They again set the tone for the younger, inexperienced group to run away with it. Even if Lawson has to make an early substitution — which also seems unlikely — she appears set on giving the vets the honor in a “it’s working” mentality. 
They went up 13-7 when Lawson subbed Boston in for Collier. Bueckers came in off the bench next for Copper, and Clark in at 4:07 for Gray with USA holding an 18-9 lead.
Lawson didn’t go completely young until the 4:02 mark of the third quarter and a 78-37 lead. The vets didn’t see the court again.
items.titleTR: Caitlin Clark-Angel Reese connection, Napheesa Collier's breakout highlight Team USA's FIBA World Cup quarterfinal win vs. Hungary

slots.packetSpot:
The United States reached the semi-finals by defeating Hungary 108-56 in the FIBA Women's World Cup quarter-finals in Berlin. Reportedly, it was the team's 34th consecutive World Cup victory; 108 points and 31 assists were also among the standout figures at quarter-final level.

Napheesa Collier was the United States' leading scorer with 19 points. Rhyne Howard recorded 15 points, while Caitlin Clark produced 10 points and 9 assists, and Angel Reese 9 points. The connection between Clark and Reese in several plays stood out as one sign of the developing chemistry among the young players.

Kara Lawson's starting five featured Chelsea Gray, Jackie Young, Kahleah Copper, Collier and Breanna Stewart; the young players received more playing time later in the game. In A'ja Wilson's absence, the United States' superiority in the paint was also evident: the team led 52-16 in the paint at the end of the game. For Hungary, Reka Lelik scored 12 points and Agnes Torok 11.

The United States will face the winner of the Spain-Australia matchup in the semi-finals.
slots.packetTitle: USA's depth on the road to the semi-finals

items.descriptionTR:
Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs
An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.
items.titleTR: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime

slots.packetSpot:
A court in Cairo sentenced television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 others to death in a case involving the production and trafficking of synthetic drugs. Khalifa’s lawyer said the defence would appeal; higher courts may uphold, reduce or overturn the sentences.

In the case, in which 28 defendants were tried, nine people were sentenced to life imprisonment and seven were acquitted. Those sentenced to death were also fined 500,000 Egyptian pounds. Before the court’s ruling, the case file had been sent to Egypt’s Grand Mufti, whose opinion is non-binding.

The prosecution alleged that Khalifa financed some parts of the operation, travelled abroad to meet senior members of the network and made contact with other members in Egypt; Khalifa denied the accusations. In the investigation that began in April 2025, authorities reported that the quantity of drugs, raw materials and equipment seized had risen from about 200 kilograms to more than 750 kilograms. Forensic examinations determined that the substances were synthetic cannabinoids.

Khalifa was also sentenced to three years in prison for assault in a separate case.
slots.packetTitle: An appeal after the death sentence
