Prime Minister Han Seong-sook on Thursday reiterated Seoul's stance that no decision has been made and various options for how to contribute to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz are on the table. "There are numerous facto
items.titleTR: 'Social consensus' needed before deployment following US request: Seoul

items.descriptionTR:
￼
The South Korea-United States alliance has been one of the principal foundations of the East Asian security architecture for more than seven decades. Established in the aftermath of the Korean War, the alliance provided South Korea with an extended security framework that enabled the country to focus on economic reconstruction, industrialization and technological development. Yet
items.titleTR: Are we seeing the end of South Korea relying on the US?

slots.packetSpot:
Washington’s request for a contribution to navigational security in the Strait of Hormuz is bringing renewed attention to the debate over South Korea’s obligations and room for manoeuvre within its alliance with the United States. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said that no decision had yet been made on military participation in the Strait of Hormuz or in the war in Ukraine; different contribution scenarios were being assessed. Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo also stated that any decision to send troops would need to take account of domestic legal procedures, National Assembly approval and social consensus.

Donald Trump is reportedly pressuring Seoul to contribute to navigational security in the strait. Trump had also shared a call for South Korea to sell its Cheongung-II missile defence system to Ukraine; this is a separate arms-export matter from possible military participation in Hormuz. Park said that the situation in Hormuz is closely linked to supply chains and to the safety of ships and South Koreans in the region. Seoul and Tokyo were also reported to be holding discussions on supply-chain disruption caused by the conflict in the Middle East, the sharing of stockpiles and energy supplies.

The debate intersects with a broader questioning of the sustainability of South Korea’s exclusive dependence on Washington. According to Asia Times’ assessment, changing US priorities, China’s regional influence, North Korea’s military capacity and South Korea’s economic and technological development are fuelling a search for greater strategic autonomy. Kim Min-seok had said on 7 September that the era of relying solely on the United States had ended. The same assessment stresses that Seoul cannot abandon the alliance at this stage; it is, however, discussing the diversification of its economic, technological, diplomatic and security partnerships.
slots.packetTitle: Seoul at the alliance's edge

items.descriptionTR:
The US and Iran are opening a new front in their six-month-old war: a battle at sea that is increasingly turning commercial shipping into a target and risks repeating the “Tanker War” of the 1980s.
The escalation follows the emergence of a tit-for-tat policy of attacks on tankers approved by US President Donald Trump that risks pulling Gulf states, outside powers and global energy markets deeper into the conflict.
The "tanker-for-tanker" tactic came into full view on Saturday, when Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships – an aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer – both of which evaded the attack.
In response, the US struck three Iranian oil tankers linked to the IRGC, disabling two and destroying a third. “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours,” US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper said.
Centcom said its latest strikes overnight targeted the IRGC-linked crude oil tankers Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, as well as Derya near Kharg Island – Iran's primary oil export hub.
Iran broadened its own attacks. On Wednesday, the IRGC said it had struck two American warships – the Delbert D Black and John Paul Jones guided-missile destroyers – along with eight oil tankers and 10 other vessels. It accused them of violating a designated “unsafe” zone around the Strait of Hormuz.
The attacks came shortly after the IRGC threatened oil tankers near the ports and harbours of Bahrain and Kuwait, whether “at anchor or berthed”. The IRGC also fired 20 ballistic missiles towards a US military base in Jordan, according to the kingdom’s armed forces, which said 18 were intercepted.
M/T Riesco sinks in the Gulf of Oman, Sept. 8, after being destroyed by CENTCOM forces in response to attempted IRGC attacks on a U.S. Navy warship. pic.twitter.com/EkmG8uyMT9
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) September 9, 2026
The result is a cycle in which each side is effectively setting the terms of the next escalation: Iran attacks US naval assets and Washington responds by hitting Iranian oil-export capacity. Then Iran expands its response to US ships, bases and commercial shipping, potentially drawing Gulf states into the conflict.
That is broadly how the 1980s Tanker War became so dangerous. Iran and Iraq attacked oil and merchant vessels to damage each other's economies, progressively drawing outside powers into the conflict and turning the security of Gulf oil into an international military concern.
'Escalatory trap'
The significance of the new tanker policy is that it changes the cost of Iran's attacks. The US is no longer simply retaliating against the military asset responsible for an attack. It is targeting an economic asset central to Iran’s ability to finance the war.
US officials have described Iran's tanker fleet as limited and exposed, while saying the vessels form part of a network that helps finance the IRGC and its regional proxies.
Iran has its own economic weapon. It has already sharply reduced shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and threatened to establish new restricted zones. Data shows daily commercial traffic in the energy chokepoint is now in the single digits, far below prewar levels when roughly 125 large commercial vessels crossed the waterway.
The 1980s showed why that matters. Once commercial shipping becomes a target, keeping the waterway open can itself become a military objective and create another means of escalation.
The US can inflict increasing damage on Iran's oil exports while Iran can make the cost and risk of moving Gulf oil increasingly high for the US and its allies. Each strike therefore creates an incentive for a more damaging response, rather than a return to the previous level of violence.
￼
The danger is no longer simply that the US and Iran might miscalculate each other’s intentions. Both sides increasingly appear to understand the other’s retaliation strategy and are responding by making each successive blow more damaging than the last.
It is a pattern that has been described as an “escalatory trap”. This was reflected in comments by Iran's Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who led the government's delegation in failed peace talks with the US but has called for the adoption of a harder line in recent weeks.
“The era of proportionate responses has ended,” Mr Ghalibaf said on Sunday. “Any violation of Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response.”
Tanker War 1.0 ended in August 1988 when a UN-brokered ceasefire halted the broader Iran-Iraq war. But with diplomatic efforts to end the 2026 conflict stalled, there are no signs that Tanker War 2.0 will end any time soon.
items.titleTR: Tanker war 2.0: How US-Iran ship attacks are escalating

slots.packetSpot:
The conflict between the United States and Iran is reportedly spreading to the sea. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed that it fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships; it later claimed to have struck two guided-missile destroyers, eight oil tankers and 10 other vessels. U.S. Central Command, meanwhile, announced that Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya were targeted in attacks on oil tankers linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps; two tankers were disabled and one was destroyed.

Iran is also reported to have threatened tankers near ports in Bahrain and Kuwait. According to Jordan’s armed forces, Iran fired 20 ballistic missiles toward a U.S. military base in the country; 18 of them were intercepted. Data indicating that commercial transits through the Strait of Hormuz fell from about 125 large vessels a day before the war to single-digit figures point to growing risk in maritime transport.

It is being assessed that reciprocal tanker attacks have turned into a “tanker-for-tanker” approach. This trajectory is said to resemble the Tanker War, which became an international military issue during the 1980s war between Iran and Iraq as commercial ships were targeted. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf also said that every violation of Iran’s interests and security would face a faster, heavier and more painful response.
slots.packetTitle: War opens a new front at sea in the Gulf

items.descriptionTR:
US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa
The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.
Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.
items.titleTR: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia

slots.packetSpot:
New ship seizures off Somalia and near Yemen are once again bringing maritime security concerns in the Gulf of Aden to the fore. According to reports, at least 13 vessels have been attacked since the start of the year; six ships were being held for ransom, four of them anchored near Bander Beyla.

It was reported that the Cameroon-flagged MV Lutuf was attacked off Puntland on 17 August, and that a few days later the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1 was seized near Yemen after pirates boarded the vessel. Accounts by the Mogadishu administration and Puntland authorities of how the MV Lutuf was released do not match: while the Somali government said a joint operation had been carried out with Türkiye, Puntland alleged that a large ransom had been paid to the pirates. These claims have not been independently verified.

The war between the United States and Iran, the struggle over the Strait of Hormuz, and the blockade around Bab el-Mandeb by the Houthis in Yemen are cited among the conditions increasing insecurity in maritime transport. Some ships sailing closer to the Somali coast to avoid the conflicts in the north, and naval patrols being diverted to other crises, may have made it easier for pirates to find targets. However, it is not yet being said that the situation has turned into a full-scale wave of piracy.

It had been stated that Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks in 2011 and held hundreds of crew members hostage. Although international naval operations and private security measures on commercial vessels reduced attacks, pirate networks are assessed to have maintained their presence because economic and security conditions in Somalia have not improved.
slots.packetTitle: Piracy reportedly returns off Somalia

items.descriptionTR:
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg on Wednesday called on the Houthis to halt missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, warning that strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure undermine efforts towards a political solution.
The Saudi ⁠Civil ⁠Defence issued alerts on Wednesday warning of a potential threat in the southern city of Khamis ⁠Mushait before saying the danger had passed.
The Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had attacked ‌an ⁠airbase in the area, which ‌lies ⁠in the ⁠south of the kingdom.
“These attacks threaten to widen the conflict, put civilians at grave risk and undermine efforts towards a political solution,” Mr Grundberg said. He called on the Houthis to halt attacks on Saudi Arabia and inside Yemen. “I call on Ansar Allah to halt these attacks, as well as its attacks inside Yemen which have also put civilians at grave risk,” he added.
He also called for an end to Houthi attacks on commercial vessels, recently condemned by the UN Security Council, saying they posed a grave risk to civilians and international shipping.
“International humanitarian law prohibits attacks directed against civilians and civilian objects,” Mr Grundberg said.
￼
The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Tuesday that at least 73 civilians were wounded in the latest escalation by the Yemeni rebels.
Saudi Arabia said the Yemeni rebels attacked energy sector sites in the kingdom's south, sparking fires, causing injuries and halting operations.
The Houthis attacked civilian and economic sites in four cities, coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said. “The attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia – the latest of which targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran – resulted in the injury of 73 civilians, including women and children,” he said.
The Houthis claimed that they struck Saudi Aramco sites in Abha, Jazan, Najran and the Economic City, along with King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, using “dozens” of ballistic missiles and drones. They said it was a response to Saudi-led strikes on Bayda, Hodeidah, Jawf, Marib and Taiz this week, and vowed further “harsher and wider” strikes unless they stopped.
The escalation comes as the conflict in Yemen becomes increasingly intertwined with the wider regional confrontation involving Iran and its allies. Saudi Arabia has sought to strengthen its defences and security partnerships as Houthi attacks have expanded beyond Yemen.
The Yemeni civil war, during which ⁠hundreds of thousands of people died from fighting and famine, has been paused under a ceasefire since 2022. But that truce broke down last month, with the Houthis effectively joining the wider war their Iranian allies have waged since being attacked by the US and Israel.
More than 22 million people require humanitarian assistance in Yemen, while 5.2 million are internally displaced and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure, according to UN data from March.
items.titleTR: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia could widen conflict, UN warns

items.descriptionTR: Yemen's government accuses Houthis of killing three children as rebels claim Saudi forces launched 54 air raids in 12 hours.
items.titleTR: Fighting escalates in Yemen; Houthi attacks trigger alerts in Saudi Arabia

slots.packetSpot:
Houthi claims of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and Saudi-led retaliatory strikes are once again carrying the war in Yemen to both sides of the border. While fires at energy facilities, temporary operational shutdowns and injuries have been reported, the parties’ accounts of airstrikes and ground fighting in Taiz, Marib, al-Jawf, Hudaydah, Saada and al-Bayda diverge.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government claims that children were killed in an artillery attack in Marib, while the Houthis maintain that there were dead and wounded in a Saudi attack on a prison in al-Jawf. The World Health Organization reports that more than 1,000 people have been killed or injured in the fighting and that tens of thousands have been displaced.

Houthi operations towards Bab el-Mandeb and the operations conducted in response are increasing the pressure exerted by the war, which has flared up again after the ceasefire, on maritime passages and Saudi Arabia’s security. Riyadh says the door to diplomacy remains open while stating that it will defend itself; the UN warns that the conflict could spread across a wider area.
slots.packetTitle: War across the border

items.titleTR: Houthis, Yemeni forces engaged in fierce battles: Why each front matters

items.descriptionTR: Yemeni media reports Houthi control of Hays and Al-Khawkhah, potentially giving group control over entire Al-Hudaydah province
items.titleTR: From Al-Hudaydah to Mocha: Rapid developments reshape Yemen’s military map

slots.packetSpot:
Fighting between the Houthis and forces loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen is intensifying on the fronts of Taiz, the west coast, Al-Jawf, Marib and Al-Dhale. According to data relayed by aid organizations, at least 194 people have been killed and 880 injured in parts of these areas over the past two weeks.

Local sources reported that, following the withdrawal of government forces, the Houthis had taken control of Hays and Al-Khawkhah in southern Al-Hudaydah and reached the Port of Mocha. There are also reports that the city of Mocha has been captured, but neither side has issued an official statement. If confirmed, these developments could strengthen the Houthis' position on the west coast and bring them closer to Bab el-Mandeb.

Government forces, meanwhile, said they had captured some areas in Al-Jawf. The fighting, described as the broadest escalation since 2022, is reopening debate over control of strategic lines along the coast and inland.
slots.packetTitle: Yemen's shifting lines of control

items.descriptionTR: Ukrainians are losing more sleep, shopping for food is becoming harder and travel is often fraught with risk and delays.
items.titleTR: Russia’s new shelling tactics deepen suffering in Ukraine

slots.packetSpot:
Russia's air attacks on Ukraine are reported to be intensifying. According to officials, four people were injured at a petrol station in Kyiv; two people were killed and 20 injured in an attack on a shopping centre in Sumy. It was announced that two people were killed and five injured in an attack on Bunge's sunflower oil plant in Dnipro; that four people were killed and around 60 injured in Pavlohrad; and that four people were killed and 19 injured in Mykolaiv.

The attacks are also reported to have targeted ports, warehouses, food suppliers, businesses, logistics networks and civilian infrastructure. Russia denies the allegation that it deliberately targets civilian sites. According to BBC Verify, which examined Ukrainian Air Force data, jet-powered drones were used every day throughout August; figures provided by the Ukrainian military show that attacks of this kind rose from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. Air defences are reported to be struggling to intercept these faster vehicles.

In Kyiv, the lengthening and increasing frequency of air raids is affecting some residents' work, children's education, transport and shopping; the psychological pressure on daily life is also described. Ukraine's counterattacks on Russian infrastructure are continuing: Russian authorities reported that eight people were injured in an attack on Sochi said to have been carried out with naval drones.
slots.packetTitle: Air war over everyday Ukraine

items.titleTR: Bundesweiter Test von Alarmsystemen an Warntag

slots.packetSpot:
In Germany, federal and state authorities activated disaster warning systems for testing purposes on 10 September, during the sixth nationwide warning day. In the exercise, which began at 11:00 a.m., channels including sirens, mobile phone alerts, Cell Broadcast, apps, digital displays, FM radio and DAB+ were used; municipalities were also able to test their own warning channels.

As municipal participation was voluntary, sirens were not expected to sound everywhere. Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Grit Tüngler, president of the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK), said in their initial assessment that the systems were able to reach broad sections of the public through different means. According to the BBK's survey last year, nearly 100 percent of participants had been reached through at least one warning channel.

This year, notifications that the danger had passed were also sent via Cell Broadcast for the first time. Warnings were also issued via DAB+. The Automatic Safety Alert system, which is intended to reach listeners by switching on radios in standby mode when mobile communications and the internet are not functioning, is planned to be launched from this month.
slots.packetTitle: Germany's warning network put to the test

items.descriptionTR:
It’s the middle of the night in April 2023 in the East China Sea.
A North Korean-linked oil tanker sailing under another country’s flag suddenly goes dark. It stops transmitting its location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS) machine that all large commercial ships have on board. It simply vanishes from the map.
Ten days later, the ship reappears on global tracking screens. Its signal places it off the coast of southern China.
Except it’s not. It’s actually in a bay many hundreds of kilometres away, preparing to deliver oil to North Korea in violation of UN sanctions.
Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations at the University of Sydney, has been tracking North Korea’s shadow fleets as part of his research.
He describes to The Conversation Weekly podcast the tactics that North Korea uses to disguise the identities of its shadow ships – and why it has got away with it for so long.
The first reason is that the oceans are a lot bigger than you think. It’s a lot harder to find ships that don’t want to be found in the ocean.
The second reason is that there is this presumption under international law that if a ship is on the high seas, you won’t really interfere with it unless you have very specific legal reasons.
Hastings compares the world’s oceans to the “Wild West” and says other countries such as Russia and Iran have now borrowed from North Korea’s playbook.
For countries that are engaging in sort of large-scale campaigns to evade sanctions, like Russia, that also have lots of money and lots of ships, boarding the ships […] is one way to at least slow them down.
But obviously there’s a lot of ships and every interdiction is really expensive and potentially dangerous.


Disclosure statement and credits
Justin Hastings does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Newsclips in this episode from BBC News and The Wall Street Journal.
This episode of The Conversation Weekly was written Justin Bergman and produced by Isabella Podwinski. Mixing by Lloyd Barrett and theme music by Neeta Sarl.

slots.packetSpot:
Sanctions enforcement at sea is being tested between methods that cause ships to lose their trail and the concrete restrictions imposed by ports. In an example described by Justin Hastings of the University of Sydney, a tanker said to be linked to North Korea switched off its AIS position signal in the East China Sea in April 2023; ten days later, it appeared in tracking systems off southern China. According to Hastings, the vessel was in fact in a bay hundreds of kilometres away, preparing to deliver oil to North Korea in violation of UN sanctions.

Hastings points to the difficulty of locating ships on the high seas and to the fact that international law requires specific legal grounds for intervention. He also says that Russia and Iran are making use of methods employed by North Korea; however, he stresses that attempts to board or stop ships can be costly and dangerous.

An example of this enforcement struggle at a port occurred in Durres. On 29 August, the Albanian Port Authority blocked the entry of the Sierra Leone-flagged Hanuman, which Ukrainian military intelligence agency GUR alleges is part of Russia’s shadow fleet. GUR reports that the tanker has carried at least 452,000 tonnes of fuel from Russia since the start of 2025; most of its voyages have run from Novorossiysk to an area near Turkey, Senegal, the United Arab Emirates and Augusta in Italy where ship-to-ship transfers take place. These claims do not mean that the port ban alone proves a sanctions violation; however, they show that ports, too, are becoming involved against opaque networks in maritime transport.
slots.packetTitle: Shadow fleets test sanctions enforcement at sea

items.descriptionTR:
Real Madrid punished two costly Inter Milan mistakes to win their Champions League opener 2-1 on Tuesday, with Kylian Mbappe and Federico Valverde scoring and goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois keeping the visitors at bay at the Santiago Bernabeu.
Erling Haaland struck twice after half-time ⁠as Manchester City won 2-0 at Porto, extending coach Enzo Maresca's winning start following three successive ⁠Premier League victories.
Real Betis twice came from behind to beat Lille 3-2 in France, with defender Marc Bartra scoring twice before Troy Parrott grabbed the winner. Lille later had Ethan Mbappe sent off.
Serhou Guirassy's late double secured Borussia Dortmund a 3-2 ⁠home victory over Villarreal after the Spanish side had cancelled out Renato Veiga's own goal.
Earlier, Aston Villa held off Club Brugge to win 3-2 in Belgium, helped by two Pau Torres assists, while Razvan Marin's free kick earned AEK Athens a 1-0 home victory over LASK.
Courtois key as Mbappe strikes
Madrid coach Jose Mourinho faced his former club at the stadium where he guided Inter to Champions League glory against Bayern Munich in 2010, but the visitors threatened to spoil his evening.
Courtois repeatedly came to their rescue against an Inter side who arguably had the better of the contest, controlling possession but paying for two costly defensive errors. The Belgian made a string of saves throughout the match to help preserve the hosts' narrow victory.
Madrid went ahead when Mbappe pressured Yann Bisseck into losing possession and Brahim Diaz collected the loose ball before feeding the French striker who sent it beneath the goalkeeper.
𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐌𝐚𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐝 𝟐-𝟏 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫  Inter had 21 shots on Tuesday; only three teams on record in the Champions League have managed more away to Real Madrid in a single game.  José Mourinho's men did enough to edge a thrilling encounter with his former club. pic.twitter.com/5aj7PqWU4h
— Opta Analyst (@OptaAnalyst) September 8, 2026
Courtois then saved Hakan Calhanoglu's powerful free kick before Inter goalkeeper Martinez gifted Real their second, attempting to dribble past Valverde inside his goal area and allowing the midfielder to poke the ball home.
Jude Bellingham missed a close-range chance before half-time and Inter maintained their pressure after the break. Carlos Augusto converted Lautaro Martinez's low cross in the 76th minute, but Real held on.
"I think we played a great first half but I don't deserve the MVP award today – Courtois deserved it because he saved us with an extraordinary performance," Valverde told Spanish broadcaster Movistar Plus.
Haaland steps up for City
City controlled possession against Porto and finished with 20 shots, including 10 on target, while the hosts failed to register a single attempt. Maresca's side forced Porto's goalkeeper into six saves before half-time but had to wait until after the break for the opener.
Haaland broke the deadlock two minutes after the restart, heading Enzo Fernandez's lofted cross into the top corner. He added his second goal a minute into stoppage time, finding the bottom corner from Rayan Ait-Nouri's pass.
“I think we could've scored more goals, especially in the first half but overall I think we deserved to win the game," Maresca told ‌Amazon Prime.
"We didn't concede a lot. It's normal to come ⁠here and concede some chances because it's normal, so overall happy with the performance."
42 - Erling Haaland has scored 42 goals in 39 appearances in the group stage/league phase of the UEFA Champions League, the most of any player since his first season in the competition in 2019-20.  Relentless. pic.twitter.com/2ivlj6b13Q
— OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) September 8, 2026
Betis trailed to Lille's 12th-minute opener before Bartra equalised from Pablo Fornals' cross. Brazilian Alexsandro restored the hosts' advantage three minutes later, following a corner.
Bartra headed in Isco's ‌free-kick in the 49th minute and Parrott completed the turnaround five minutes later with a low strike after an individual run.
Elsewhere, Dortmund went ahead through Veiga's attempted clearance in the 53rd minute before Villarreal levelled with a close-range header in the 66th. Guirassy restored the lead from Fabio Silva's pass in the 80th and converted a penalty four minutes later after being fouled, before scoring an own goal in added time while trying to help in defence.
Villa edge to victory in Belgium
In Belgium, Torres set up John McGinn to put Aston Villa ahead against Brugge in the 11th minute, but Hugo Vetlesen equalised for the hosts eight minutes later.
Villa responded swiftly, with Emiliano Buendia restoring their lead from a Joao Gomes assist before Nicolas Jackson made it 3-1 just before half-time, Torres again supplying the final pass.
Brugge dominated after the break, and Nicolo Tresoldi pulled a goal back with a penalty in the 61st minute, but Villa protected their advantage to secure all three points.
Marin provided the decisive moment for AEK in the 21st minute against Austria's LASK, curling a free kick from outside the penalty area on the left-hand side into the top corner beyond the goalkeeper's reach.
items.titleTR: Mbappe and Courtois key as Real Madrid survive Inter scare, Haaland hits double for Man City

items.descriptionTR:
In an interview with RAC1 (h/t Mundo Deportivo), FC Barcelona sporting director Deco claimed that he has no doubts about who should win the next Ballon d’Or, insisting that the top prize should go t...
￼
Barcelona director backs Lamine Yamal to win the Ballon d’Or: ‘I see no doubt about it’

In an interview with RAC1 (h/t Mundo Deportivo), FC Barcelona sporting director Deco claimed that he has no doubts about who should win the next Ballon d’Or, insisting that the top prize should go to Lamine Yamal.

The Barcelona sporting director made his position clear openly backing Lamine to win the Golden Orb, while also questioning the decision to leave Pedri and Raphinha off the list of nominees.

“I think Lamine is the top candidate. I see no doubt about it,” said Deco.

Deco believes Lamine’s performances over the past season make him the standout candidate. The winger played a decisive role in Barcelona’s campaign and continued to impress despite arriving at the World Cup after recovering from an injury.

“He had a great season with Barça and went to the World Cup after an injury. Last season he was key to winning La Liga.”

The Barcelona sporting director even brought Lionel Messi into the discussion to underline his belief that Lamine deserves the award.
￼
Will Lamine win the Ballon d’Or? (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

“I like football. It’s like when Leo was winning and Leo was the best. In this case, there isn’t much to discuss,” he firmly stated.

Lamine is among the 30 nominees for the 2026 Ballon d’Or, alongside a host of major names including Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Jr., Harry Kane, Erling Haaland, Messi, as well as Barcelona duo Rodri and Pau Cubarsi.

For Deco, however, Lamine stands above the rest.

The same sentiment was echoed by Barcelona manager Hansi Flick after the team’s 5-1 win over Feyenoord on Wednesday, with Lamine scoring a sensational goal.

“He’s my player, so of course I do. He deserves to win the Ballon d’Or. He’s an exceptional, special player. Anyone who watches his matches knows he deserves it,” Flick said.
￼
Lamine finished as a runner-up in the 2025 Ballon d’Or. (Photo by Alex Caparros/Getty Images)
Pedri and Raphinha omissions labelled “a global scandal”

If Deco was emphatic about Lamine, he was even more critical when discussing the absence of two of his teammates.

The sporting director described it as “a global scandal” that Pedri and Raphinha did not make the Ballon d’Or shortlist.

“It’s a global scandal. I don’t understand the shortlists. Individual awards are unfair. Football is a team sport; it’s difficult to single out individuals,” he said.

“Seeing that Pedri isn’t on the list, given the talent he has, I just don’t get it,” Deco added.
items.titleTR: Barcelona director backs Lamine Yamal to win the Ballon d’Or: ‘I see no doubt about it’

slots.packetSpot:
The 30-man shortlist for the 2026 Ballon d’Or was announced on 8 September; the winner will be revealed at the ceremony in London on 26 October. The 2025 winner, Ousmane Dembélé, leads the Paris Saint-Germain contingent, which has nine players on the list.

Achraf Hakimi and Sadio Mané are the two nominees from Africa. Africa’s only Ballon d’Or winner was George Weah in 1995; Mané’s second-place finish in 2022 stands out as the continent’s best result since then. Hakimi or Mané appear to have limited chances of lifting the trophy this year.

Barcelona sporting director Deco said in an interview with RAC1, reported by Mundo Deportivo, that he sees Lamine Yamal as the strongest candidate. Deco also described Pedri and Raphinha’s absence from the shortlist as a “global scandal”. Barcelona head coach Hansi Flick also stated that Yamal deserves the award.

items.descriptionTR: Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka will bid to move one step closer to a third straight US Open title when she faces familiar foe ‌Jessica Pegula, while Elena Rybakina will take on home favourite Coco Gauff in the semi-finals on Thursday from midnight - live on Sky Sports Tennis.
items.titleTR: Top four in the world set for US Open semi-finals showdown

items.descriptionTR:
The US Open comes to a conclusion in New York this weekend and the final four in both the men's and women's singles are now set.
The men's draw has been wide open, largely thanks to the absence of world No 1 Jannik Sinner and the fitness problems of Carlos Alcaraz, who bowed out in the last eight.
Alexander Zverev will be the favourite from here, but he will have to overcome an American player and the home crowd in the final if he can first get past Karen Khachanov.
The women's line-up has plenty of stardust after the top four seeds all made the semi-finals for the first time at a Grand Slam since Wimbledon in 2009.
Women's singles
Aryna Sabalenka (1) v Jessica Pegula (3)
The first of the semi-finals is one we have seen before in New York. This is a repeat of the 2024 final and a semi-final from last year. Sabalenka won both of those matches.
Since then, Pegula has won two of their three meetings, on grass in Berlin and on the hard court in Wuhan, while Sabalenka chalked up a victory over the American at the WTA Finals in Riyadh.
Pegula is a problem solver and will have analysed where she went wrong the last two times in New York, while Sabalenka looked vulnerable when squeaking through against Linda Noskova on Tuesday. Pegula can cause a mini upset here, but it's going to be a brutal contest and almost certain to go the distance.
Pick: Pegula in three
Elena Rybakina (2) v Coco Gauff (4)
Gauff is such a fighter and knows how to use the energy of the home crowd, so can never truly be ruled out. However, putting the intangibles to one side, it would be a minor shock if she got past Rybakina, who is now most people's favourite for the title, and will take the world No 1 spot next week.
The 27-year-old is a dominant force on the hard court when her serve is firing, as it has been over the past 10 days. Naomi Osaka had no answer in the last 16 before a battling Zheng Qinwen submitted to the power of her serve and ruthless groundstrokes in the quarter-finals.
Pick: Rybakina in two
Men's singles
Alexander Zverev (1) v Karen Khachanov
Zverev has reached the semi-finals at all four majors this year and is the only Grand Slam winner left standing in the men's draw.
The French Open champion and Wimbledon runner-up would probably view it as a failure if he didn't go on and claim a second major title from this point.
Zverev leads the head-to-head 6-3 and has won four of the last five against Khachanov.
Pick: Zverev in four
Frances Tiafoe (11) v Ben Shelton (8)
This all-American showdown will – much to the delight of the US crowd – guarantee a home player in the final.
For both, it will be a third major semi-final of their careers, with Tiafoe a last-four loser twice in New York, and Shelton having made the semis in Australia and the US.
The 23-year-old Shelton leads their head-to-head 3-1 and seems to have all the momentum after his big win over Carlos Alcaraz. Can't see it being easy, though.
Pick: Shelton in five
items.titleTR: US Open semi-final predictions: Zverev and Shelton look strong, Pegula to upset Sabalenka

slots.packetSpot:
The 2026 US Open presents two distinct semifinal pictures. In the women’s draw, the top four seeds — Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula, Elena Rybakina and Coco Gauff — have reached the last four. This is happening at a Grand Slam for the first time since Wimbledon 2009, while at the US Open it is occurring for only the second time in the Open Era, after 1975.

Sabalenka will face Pegula, while Rybakina will meet Gauff. Rybakina is said to be set to rise to world No. 1 next week.

In the men’s draw, the Alexander Zverev–Karen Khachanov and Ben Shelton–Frances Tiafoe semifinals have been set. Zverev advanced by defeating Botic van de Zandschulp; Khachanov reached the semifinals after Alexander Blockx withdrew from the match. Tiafoe beat Alex Michelsen, while Shelton overcame Carlos Alcaraz. The absence of world No. 1 Jannik Sinner and Alcaraz’s quarterfinal elimination are cited among the factors making the men’s draw a more open contest.

The 2026 Solheim Cup, to be played near Bernardus Golf Club from 11 to 13 September, brings Europe and the United States together in the Netherlands. Each of the last three editions held in Europe ended with no more than a one-point margin: the United States won by one point in Germany in 2015, Europe prevailed by one point at Gleneagles in 2019; in the 14-14 draw in Spain, the trophy remained with Europe. The aggregate score across those three encounters is 42-42.

The pressure of the home crowd, weather conditions and the difficulty of Bernardus are among the factors standing out ahead of the contest. Charley Hull says playing at home can create more pressure, while Nelly Korda states that the United States will need mental resilience to win in Europe. Roel Verdonschot believes that the 15th and 18th holes in particular have the qualities to create drama late in matches.

The controversy in 2015 is also being recalled; whether a similar moment will occur remains uncertain. In the three-day schedule beginning on Friday, foursomes and fourball matches will be followed by 12 singles matches on Sunday.

items.titleTR: Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut

slots.packetSpot:
Ryan Garcia's absence from the planned face-off at Mandalay Bay on Tuesday, ahead of his WBC welterweight title fight with Conor Benn in Las Vegas, sparked public debate. Garcia said he did not attend because he wanted to maintain his routine, while Benn described it as disrespectful to the spectators; Benn later faced off jokingly with his father, Nigel Benn.

Benn says trying to get down to the 147-pound/67-kilogram welterweight limit for the first time in more than four years has been extremely difficult, but that he is healthy and will make the limit at Friday's weigh-in. Garcia said his own weight cut had been easy, voiced doubts about Benn's situation and stated that he did not want to hear excuses about weight cutting after the fight. Carl Froch and Chris Algieri were also among those questioning whether Benn's return to welterweight would wear him down.

Garcia is scheduled to defend his title for the first time on Saturday at T-Mobile Arena, while Benn is set to contest his first world championship fight. Manager is excited by new US deal but might have returned to Spurs if the stars had aligned and does not rule out taking England job one day
If things had worked out differently, Mauricio Pochettino would have gone back to his beloved Tottenham over the summer. They had put in the call and it stirred him. Nothing was going to put him off – not even the possibility of the club being in the Championship.
Seriously, Mauricio? After a World Cup campaign with the United States and top jobs with Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain before that, he would have been willing to start a new chapter in the second tier of English football? “Yes, of course,” Pochettino says. “Tottenham … it’s the only club that always I am open to help. In whatever division.”
items.titleTR: Mauricio Pochettino: ‘I am always open to help Tottenham. In whatever division’

slots.packetSpot:
Mauricio Pochettino says he hopes to return to English football in the future. He states that Tottenham contacted him, but that he could not return because he has a contract with the United States and is preparing for the World Cup; he adds that if the timing is right, he would be open to helping the club in any league.

Pochettino, who signed a new four-year contract with the United States running until the 2030 World Cup, says he could consider the possibility of managing the England national team only in the future, if he is available and receives an offer. He particularly underlines that it is not currently on his agenda.

items.descriptionTR:
Seattle's defense and receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba had huge games against the Patriots on Wednesday.
The Seattle Seahawks are defending Super Bowl champions and defended their title in Week 1 despite adversity. Despite losing starting quarterback Sam Darnold in their first offensive series, the Seahawks came back from a 10-0 deficit to defeat the New England Patriots 13-10 on Wednesday in a rematch of the Super Bowl to open the 2026 FNL regular season.
That gives them the initial lead in the NFC West before they face the Arizona Cardinals next week in Week 2.
Offensively, it was a struggle. They punted or had the first half end in their first six possessions. But backup Drew Lock threw a touchdown pass to reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the second half, and kicker Jason Myers made two field goals, including the game-winner with 5:50 left in the game.
The Seahawks only had 285 yards of offense against New England, but Smith-Njigba had eight receptions for 122 yards and a touchdown. The rest of the Seahawks pass catchers combined for nine receptions for 78 yards.
Rookie running back Jadarian Price rushed for 52 yards on 10 attempts.
But the defense held the Patriots to 277 yards and picked off Drake Maye in three straight possessions in the fourth quarter. Josh Jobe intercepted Maye in the end zone with 21 seconds left in the game.
The Seahawks defense picked off three passes, had three sacks, nine tackles for loss and six pass breakups.
The defending champions made a statement in Week 1. That defense is still fierce, and they can still win tough games, even with their backup quarterback.

The Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots 13-10 in the opening game of the 2026 NFL regular season, winning the Super Bowl LX rematch. The Patriots led 10-0 late in the third quarter; Seattle came back with 13 unanswered points.

Sam Darnold left the game with a hip injury on Seattle's first offensive series. Drew Lock, who replaced him, completed 16 of 22 passes and threw a touchdown pass. Mike Macdonald said Darnold had not suffered a hip fracture, but that further tests were needed to determine the severity of the injury.

Seattle's defense allowed 277 yards and forced three turnovers. Drake Maye threw three interceptions in the fourth quarter; one came in the end zone late in the game. Jaxon Smith-Njigba produced 122 yards on eight receptions and a 45-yard touchdown. For New England, A.J. Brown left the game with an ankle injury and did not return.

items.descriptionTR: Formula 1 debuts a new circuit to its calendar, and despite no grand prix raced yet, the Madring already boasts a corner that is poised to become an iconic scene in motorsport.
items.titleTR: F1 debuts a new track with a corner so grand it is called Monumental

slots.packetSpot:
The Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix is moving to Madrid; the new Madring circuit is contracted to host the event until 2035. Returning to the capital after Barcelona, the race also stands out through Madrid's ambition to broaden a sporting identity associated with football.

With 22 corners combining public roads and private land, Madring is both a street circuit and a purpose-built track. Turn 12, La Monumental, is at the centre of the design with its long, banked 270-degree layout. While different figures have been given for the corner's banking, drivers and officials regard it as a fast, challenging section that could create overtaking opportunities.

According to the BBC, the circuit will be powered by renewable energy, and some existing structures in the surrounding area will also be used. It is reported that €65 million has been invested in additional construction and €85 million in the circuit itself; space is planned for more than 30,000 spectators around La Monumental. Madrid last hosted a Formula 1 race in 1981.

Rory McIlroy believes traditional tours will soon have “decisions to make” as a player exodus from LIV Golf edges closer. LIV filing for bankruptcy in the United States on Tuesday means its deals with several high-profile golfers will soon be invalid, leaving them free to negotiate a route back to the PGA and DP World Tours.
When asked whether remaining with LIV in its planned, far-less lucrative form would hold appeal, McIlroy was characteristically candid. “I’m not in their shoes but LIV at the start looked a lot more attractive than what LIV 2.0 might be from a financial standpoint,” said the Masters champion.

slots.packetSpot:
LIV Golf’s reported bankruptcy filing in the United States and the final event of its current form in 2026 have carried the circuit’s future into an uncertain transition. After Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund withdrew its funding, a smaller and financially tighter LIV 2.0 is being envisaged with a potential investor linked to BC Partners; whether it will come to fruition appears to depend on players’ decisions.

Rory McIlroy said he expects some players to leave, adding that the PGA Tour and DP World Tour may need to decide how to respond to possible returns. The direction of Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Cameron Smith is a matter of speculation; Bryson DeChambeau is widely expected to stay, while Lee Westwood said he would decide after seeing the new structure. There is still no clarity over players’ contracts, their options on other tours and LIV’s sustainability.

items.descriptionTR:
The trial has caused heated debate in women’s rugby, with England’s Zoe Harrison calling it the ‘worst decision ever’, but others more open to it
“We won a World Cup with a size five so it can’t have been that bad,” the England full-back Ellie Kildunne says of World Rugby’s trial with smaller balls in the upcoming WXV Global Series. The top 12 nations in the world rankings will be playing home and away matches from Saturday with the WXV competition revamped from the one contested over the past few years. There will be no trophy at the end of it and the ball trial that has produced no little debate is in place.
Players will compete with a size 4.5 ball instead ofthe aforementioned size five, which is used across rugby union; the new ball weighs the same but is 3% smaller. The reasoning is to see if a smaller ball will improve skillsets because of women’s physiology, despite statistics such as a 87.8% lineout success rate at the 2025 Women’s Six Nations and kicking success at goal reaching 61% at the World Cup last year with the old ball.
items.titleTR: The Breakdown | How the smaller ball trial in WXV has brought ‘mixed bag of emotions’

slots.packetSpot:
The smaller ball World Rugby is trialling in women’s international rugby is prompting sharply divided reactions among players. The trial is not a permanent change; it is intended to test whether a smaller ball improves skills.

The size 4.5 ball used in the WXV Global Series is 3% smaller than the standard size 5 ball, but weighs the same. Following positive feedback from youth tournaments and the Sevens World Series, the measure has been taken to elite Test level, with players expected to give their views at the end of the competition, by the end of October.

England’s Zoe Harrison described the decision as “the worst decision ever”, while Wales hooker Kelsey Jones said she had needed to alter her throwing technique to get used to the ball and had mixed feelings. England full-back Ellie Kildunne said ball control had not changed greatly, although spiral kicks had become more difficult; nevertheless, she said she did not expect serious problems.

With the standard ball, line-out success reached 87.8% in the 2025 Women’s Six Nations, while goal-kicking success reached 61% at last year’s World Cup. These figures show not the superiority of the smaller ball, but the existing performance level surrounding the question World Rugby wants to test.
slots.packetTitle: A smaller ball, a bigger debate

Steve Borthwick will be handed a contract extension until after the 2028 Six Nations, giving the Rugby Football Union time to identify his successor if England flop at the World Cup next year.
The RFU’s move is designed to avoid uncertainty heading into the tournament but stops short of backing Borthwick in the long-term.
items.titleTR: England to extend Borthwick contract as Pollock closes on £400,000 Northampton deal

slots.packetSpot:
The Rugby Football Union has reportedly extended Steve Borthwick’s contract as head coach of England’s men’s national team beyond the 2027 World Cup, until the end of the 2028 Six Nations. Conor O’Shea said the decision, which came after England won only one match in the 2026 Six Nations, was intended to provide the coaching staff with security ahead of the World Cup while buying time to assess options after the tournament.

Borthwick took up the role in December 2022. The report says the extension is not seen as a sign of long-term, strong backing; the RFU is continuing succession planning for the next head coach.
slots.packetTitle: Borthwick secured through the World Cup

It's no secret that the National Football League has designs on global expansion. This season, the NFL will host a record nine regular-season games abroad, returning to Europe for six games, Mexico for one, and hosting a first-ever game in Australia.
items.titleTR: What to Expect from the NFL in Brazil in September

items.descriptionTR: The NFL will open its 2026 season with a match in Melbourne, Australia, this week, one of a record nine matches to take place overseas this season. And it shows no signs of slowing down yet.
items.titleTR: The NFL's MCG takeover just the latest step towards global domination

slots.packetSpot:
The number of NFL games to be played outside the United States in the 2026 regular season is rising to a record nine. In a schedule spanning Brazil, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Mexico and Australia, Melbourne will host an NFL regular-season game for the first time; Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens will also face each other at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro.

According to ABC, the NFL had played 62 regular-season games outside the United States before the 2026 season. Brazil had previously hosted games in São Paulo in 2024 and 2025. The NFL confirmed that 10 overseas games will be played in 2027.

Commissioner Roger Goodell said his goal is to raise the number of international games to 16 and that he believes NFL teams will one day be based outside the United States as well. The league's Global Markets Program, its local office in Australia and its International Academy on the Gold Coast are among the elements of its strategy to grow fan relationships in international markets. It is also reported that the Victoria government is spending between $10 million and $15 million on each game in Melbourne, with expectations that this will be recouped through tourism revenue.
slots.packetTitle: The NFL plays beyond borders

items.descriptionTR:
A $150,000 prize in Budapest has the record-breaking Scot buzzing but the middle-distance star insists he’s no longer chasing paydays
The richest event in track and field history launches in Budapest this weekend, and the prospect of walking away with $150,000 at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship has got Josh Kerr ready to rumble again, on and off the track.
Some critics have noted that the Scot has run only five times in 2026 – compared with Amy Hunt’s 43 races – and has had to rely on a wild card from World Athletics to even compete in Budapest.
items.titleTR: ‘I’m not a robot’: Josh Kerr primed to peak against arch rival Ingebrigtsen

slots.packetSpot:
Josh Kerr is preparing for the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest after criticism over his limited number of races. Jakob Ingebrigtsen is scheduled to compete in the 5,000 metres on Friday and in the 1,500-metre final with Kerr on Sunday.

Kerr was criticised for having raced on the track only five times in 2026 and for not taking part in the European Championships in Birmingham last month. It was also reported that he relied on a wild card from World Athletics to compete in Budapest. The Scottish athlete says that in four of his races he broke the world mile record, set a personal best in the 800 metres, and won gold in the 3,000 metres at the World Indoor Championships and in the 1,500 metres at the Commonwealth Games. He says he chooses two to four major race dates a year and wants to run only when he is ready.

The new, three-day Ultimate Championship has a total prize fund of $10 million; the prize in Budapest is $150,000. Kerr says he is pleased that Ingebrigtsen is racing again and considers him one of the greatest 1,500- and 5,000-metre runners of all time. Kerr, 28, who won his first world title in Budapest in 2023, says he expects to win again this time and aims to become the best 1,500-metre runner of his generation, and even of all time. Cole Hocker and Cameron Myers are also in the field.
slots.packetTitle: Face to face again in Budapest

Although the official opening ceremony of the 20th Asian Games will be held on 19 September, the men's basketball tournament has begun in Nagoya. In the opening group matches at Aichi International Arena, Qatar beat Iran 59-35, while South Korea defeated Saudi Arabia 82-66.

Michael Lewis scored 21 points for Qatar, while Lee Hyun-jung had 23 for South Korea. In the tournament, where 12 teams are divided into three groups, the medal matches will be played on 20 September; the Games in Nagoya-Aichi will continue until 4 October.

items.descriptionTR: Apple says its new watches won’t save raw audio, but features that can transcribe recent speech and summarize ambient conversations raise new questions about consent, privacy, and how people behave when they know they could always be recorded.
items.titleTR: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening

slots.packetSpot:
As the use of sensors that perceive their surroundings and artificial intelligence expands in Apple’s wearable devices, promises of benefit and accessibility are also amplifying questions of privacy, consent and social acceptance. According to Mark Gurman’s reporting in Bloomberg, rumours of camera-equipped AirPods have been pushed back to 2027; it is suggested that these cameras are intended not so much for taking ordinary photos or videos as for feeding Siri AI and Visual Intelligence.

Audio Intelligence, added to the Apple Watch, can process live sound and provide alerts for certain sounds. When enabled, Live Rewind can transcribe what was said in the previous 15 seconds; Siri Recap can generate titles, summaries and key points from conversations in the surrounding environment. Apple states that Siri Recap is not continuously on by default, can be turned on and off, does not create or retain raw audio recordings, does not identify speakers, and end-to-end encrypts the generated text and summaries.

While these features may benefit people who are deaf or hard of hearing, the possibility that nearby conversations may be turned into text or summaries raises questions of consent and law. Camera-equipped AirPods are not yet a confirmed product; nevertheless, the direction of wearable devices towards interpreting environmental information is sharpening the debate over how these technologies will be received in everyday life.
slots.packetTitle: An ear on the wrist

items.descriptionTR: Apple introduced Apple Reference Image to help users determine whether photos have been edited, including alterations made by AI.
items.titleTR: Apple has a new way to prove your iPhone photos aren’t AI slop

items.descriptionTR: A new study by two MIT researchers puts forward a framework for addressing just how difficult it may be to definitively connect an AI-generated image to any specific source material
items.titleTR: ‘Attribution decay’ complicates the picture of AI-generated images, scientists find

slots.packetSpot:
Two distinct traceability problems stand out in images involving artificial intelligence: how a photograph was taken and whether it was subsequently altered; and the extent to which a generated image can be linked to a particular piece of training data.

Apple announced a feature called Apple Reference Image for photographs taken with the iPhone 18 Pro. According to the company’s statement, the main camera sensor also records signed sensor data; Private Cloud Compute turns this data into an unalterable reference image that can be viewed in the Photos app. Apple says this reference could help identify changes by comparing it with other versions of the photograph. It was also announced that APIs would be offered to developers and that the SynthID standard for identifying AI-generated or altered images would be supported.

A study published in Nature Communications by Zheng Dai and David K. Gifford of MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, meanwhile, indicates that the influence of individual sources may become blurred in large training datasets. In the phenomenon the researchers call “attribution erosion,” removing a particular item from the training set may not meaningfully change the generated image. This makes it more complicated to link an output to a particular training image and to address copyright debates; however, the researchers’ findings do not exonerate the training process or, on their own, resolve questions of infringement.
slots.packetTitle: Where the image trail fades

The WMO and SAWS warn that El Niño is intensifying into a potentially record-breaking event, bringing severe heatwaves, low rainfall, and elevated drought risks to South Africa this summer.
The WMO and SAWS warn that El Niño is intensifying into a potentially record-breaking event, bringing severe heatwaves, low rainfall, and elevated drought risks to South Africa this summer.
items.titleTR: El Niño set to strengthen into very strong event, WMO says

items.descriptionTR: A hotter, drier summer could bring food insecurity, unsafe water, heat illness and infectious disease outbreaks. We cannot claim these consequences were unforeseen.
items.titleTR: El Niño is here: South Africa must pay for prevention now

slots.packetSpot:
The World Meteorological Organization expects El Niño to strengthen and become a very strong event toward the end of the year. The South African Weather Service forecasts below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures across much of the country during the October 2026–January 2027 period, while warning of possible severe heatwaves.

The agriculture ministry states that low rainfall and high temperatures could lead to drought conditions, heat stress, crop losses and livestock deaths; water restrictions could also affect irrigating farmers. Risk-reduction measures are recommended, including prioritising varieties resilient to dry and hot conditions and avoiding unnecessary expansion of production areas.

However, the World Meteorological Organization stresses that the intensity of El Niño does not automatically determine the severity of impacts in South Africa. El Niño is a natural ocean-atmosphere phenomenon; it is not caused by climate change, but its effects occur under conditions of global warming.
slots.packetTitle: A hot, dry summer looms over South Africa

items.descriptionTR:
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the African Union (AU) Commission renewed their longstanding strategic partnership today with the signing of an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva. This renewed agreement reaffirms the joint commitment to advancing health security, universal health coverage, and sustainable development across the African continent at a time of unprecedented financial challenges in the global health landscape.
It further underscores the African Union’s leadership in fostering collective action, inclusive partnerships, and regional resilience, and positions the Department of Health, Humanitarian Affairs, and Social Development of the AU Commission at the heart of the continent’s health policy implementation efforts.
The agreement was signed by Her Excellency Ambassador Amma Adomaa Twum-Amoah, Commissioner for Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development, on behalf of His Excellency Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African Union Commission, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. It marks a defining moment for primary health care and universal health coverage.
Commissioner Twum-Amoah emphasized the strategic importance of the agreement and the AU’s leadership in shaping Africa’s health landscape:
“This Agreement marks a new chapter in AU–WHO cooperation. By working together more closely, we can better respond to the health needs of our populations and ensure that no one is left behind. The African Union values WHO’s central and leading role in global health and looks forward to deepening this strategic partnership in support of our shared goals. We need to move from budgeting for survival to planning for health sovereignty,” she added.
Building on the foundation of the 2019 MoU, the renewed agreement streamlines and strengthens collaboration across all AU entities. It aligns efforts in support of Africa’s health priorities and sets the stage for enhanced cooperation between WHO and the AU. It also reaffirms WHO’s central technical and normative leadership role in global and regional health, and its commitment to supporting the AU and its institutions in achieving health-related Sustainable Development Goals.
“This renewed agreement comes at a critical time, as cuts to bilateral aid imperil the health of millions in Africa,” said Dr Tedros. “It reflects our determination to translate our partnership into tangible results for the people of Africa, and support countries to leave behind the era of aid dependency and transition to sustainable self-reliance. We are proud to stand with the African Union in driving forward the health priorities of the continent.”
The Memorandum outlines five key areas of collaboration:
	•	health systems strengthening: including regulatory harmonization, support for local pharmaceutical manufacturing, traditional medicine, domestic health financing, workforce development, and digital health innovation;
	•	reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child, and adolescent health (RMNCAH): with continued support for the Campaign on Accelerated Reduction of Maternal Mortality in Africa (CARMMA Plus 2021–2030) and advancement of the reviewed Addis Ababa Declaration on Immunization (ADi);
	•	disease prevention and control: supporting the implementation of AU frameworks on communicable and noncommunicable diseases, including efforts to end AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria; eliminate neglected tropical diseases (NTDs); and address the burden of viral hepatitis in line with WHO strategies;
	•	nutrition and food security: strengthening the nutrition agenda through implementation of the Africa Nutrition Strategy 2015–2025 and related WHO strategies; and
	•	health in emergency settings: by strengthening joint responses to humanitarian crises, conflicts, and climate-related emergencies.
The timing of the renewed agreement is significant. It reflects the African Union’s elevated voice in global health governance – bolstered by its G20 membership – and highlights WHO’s ongoing key role as a trusted technical and operational partner.
The renewed MoU marks new momentum for regional and multilateral cooperation to address Africa’s most pressing health challenges and deliver meaningful, lasting results on the continent.
For further information:
Professor Julio Rakotonirina | Director | Department of Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development | African Union Commission | E-mail JulioR@africa-union.org   
Ms Stéphanie Seydoux | Director | DG Envoy for Multilateral Affairs| World Health Organization| E-mail seydouxs@who.int
items.titleTR: African Union and World Health Organization renew strategic partnership to drive impact and strengthen health systems in Africa
